one_sentence_summary: Swift 기반 네이티브 ROS 2 지원 및 LeRobot 차이 분석 CLI 공개와 함께 추론 엔진·검색 API·오픈소스 모델 확장이 이어졌습니다.
weekly_themes: - 해석: 물리 로봇 제어 분야에서 비디오 기반 파운데이션 모델 및 월드 모델 가상 합성 데이터를 활용해 범용 작업 적응성을 높이려는 파이프라인 개발이 구체화되고 있습니다 [77, 79].
section_robotics:
- **Swift-ros2 3.0**: 별도의 브리지나 rcl 크로스 컴파일 없이 Zenoh 또는 DDS를 통해 Swift 앱이 ROS 2 그래프에 직접 참여하도록 지원하며, swift-ros2-rosidl 등 세 패키지로 분리되어 독립 GitHub 조직으로 이전되었습니다 [19].
- **robot-data-diff**: LeRobot 데이터셋의 두 리비전을 비교하여 에피소드 변경 내역과 액션 통계 및 유휴 비율을 HTML 리포트로 출력하는 도구로, 비디오 다운로드 없이 CPU만으로 동작합니다 [20].
- **NVIDIA Cosmos**: 자율주행 및 결함 이미지 생성 등 5가지 클라우드 네이티브 블루프린트를 Data Factory에 추가하고, 시뮬레이션 환경에서 자율주행 정책과 양팔 로봇 제어를 검증하는 Cosmos 3 Nano 모델 변형을 제공합니다 [79].
section_devtools:
- **DeepInfer**: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 모델을 지원하는 오픈소스 추론 프레임워크로, NVIDIA SM100 GPU 및 Huawei Ascend 950 NPU 지원과 함께 FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, DeepEP 커널 및 비동기 스케줄링을 Apache 2.0 라이선스로 제공합니다 [42].
- **DeepSeek Search 및 Fetch API**: 구조화된 웹 검색 결과와 단일 웹페이지 마크다운 추출을 제공하는 API로, 토큰 수가 아닌 성공한 요청 1,000건당 0.75달러로 과금됩니다 [11].
- **Recursive Flint**: Apache 2.0 라이선스의 40B MoE 모델(토큰당 약 2.5B 활성화)로 262K 컨텍스트를 지원하며, RTX Spark, DGX Spark, GeForce RTX 등 로컬 하드웨어 실행에 최적화되었습니다 [62, 66].
- **MCP Servers v2.0.0**: 레거시 클라이언트 호환성을 유지하면서 modern era 스펙을 지원하도록 공식 서버 구조를 리팩터링하였으며, TypeScript 기반 서버의 Node.js 요구 사양을 Node 24로 상향했습니다 [26].
- **Anthropic Agent Skills**: 벤더 중립성을 확보하기 위해 Agent Skills 표준을 리눅스 재단 산하 Agentic AI Foundation(AAIF)에 기증했습니다 [75].
- **LiteLLM 1.107.0 PyPI 공급망 침해**: PyPI에 등록되었던 1.107.0 휠 파일에 자격증명 탈취기(cook.py)와 원격 코드 실행 백도어(sitecustomize.py)가 포함되어 제거되었으며, 업스트림 소스와 1.106.2 및 RC 버전은 영향을 받지 않았습니다 [58].
section_industry:
- **Agility Robotics Digit 5**: 23kg 빈을 들어 올릴 수 있고 9분 충전으로 90분 구동 가능한 배터리를 갖추도록 설계된 Digit 5를 공개했으며, AGCO의 캔자스주 헤스턴 공장에 2027년부터 투입하는 상용 파일럿 계약을 체결했습니다 [27, 64].
- **Dream Labs**: 9,000만 달러 규모의 시드 투자를 유치하고 카메라 영상과 자연어 명령을 모터 제어로 변환하는 Dream API를 출시했으며, 주력 모델인 Dream-1은 그리퍼가 달린 양팔 로봇에 대해 제로샷 학습을 지원합니다 [77].
- **Kodama Systems**: 산림 및 임업 장비 자율화를 위해 700만 달러를 추가 유치했으며, 원격 조작과 감독형 자율성을 결합해 상용 벌목 현장의 스키더 장비에 적용하고 있습니다 [30].
- **OpenAI의 Orchestra Bio 인수**: 생명과학 R&D 분야에 AI 기반 운영을 도입하고 신약 개발을 가속하기 위해 Orchestra Bio 인수를 발표했습니다 [39].
- **OpenAI-Google Cloud 파트너십**: OpenAI의 프론티어 모델과 Codex 워크플로를 Google Cloud Marketplace 및 모델 가든을 통해 배포하기로 협력했습니다 [57, 60].

global_items.title: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
global_items.summary: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. — Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang , How the Claude Code team does code review Tags: anthropic , claude , ai , claude-code , llms , addy-osmani , coding-agents , generative-ai , agentic-engineering , code-review

global_items.articleText: Tool: LaTeX renderer Simon Willison’s Weblog Newsletter Sponsored by: Teleport — AI agents (and sub-agents they spawn) are given the same access as humans, but they never sleep. Learn how to monitor and constrain their behavior with isolated ephemeral trusted runtimes. 15th October 2026 Tool LaTeX renderer — LaTeX renderer turns LaTeX source into a rendered view, either a single display equation typeset by MathJax or a full document or prose fragment typeset by faster-latex, with a live preview beside the editor and a toolbar switch between Edit and Rendered views. Source can be typed, loaded from a URL or GitHub Gist, or picked from built-in examples, and the page keeps the LaTeX in the URL fragment so it can be shared as a readable or compressed link. Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks: Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well: We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool Here's an example link . The tool uses Pako 2.1.0 , MathJax 4.1.3 , faster-latex 0.3.1 , and DOMPurify 3.4.16 . global_items.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents: LLM agents that think in latent space, act through text
global_items.articleText: Computer Science > Computation and Language arXiv:2610.18861 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Oct 2026] Title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents Authors: Jiaru Zou , Yunzhe Qi , Sirui Chen , Federico Bianchi , Shang Zhu , Pan Lu , Jingrui He , James Zou View a PDF of the paper titled Hybrid Reasoning Agents, by Jiaru Zou and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at this https URL . global_items.title: I built a programming language that LLMs can't use
global_items.articleText: Writing code is probably something LLMs have excelled at the most. But how much of their ability to write code is due to their understanding of it vs. just them recalling code snippets which were present in their training dataset or their context window? This is what I set out to answer. In order to do so I decided to design and implement a programming language which, while usable for humans, should be as difficult for LLMs and coding agents as possible. I figured testing an LLM’s ability to understand and write code in a programming language that it has never seen before was a good start. But I also wanted to include features in the language which exploit the weaknesses of LLMs. For example, their apparent difficulty in counting letters, their over eager safety guard rails and their keenness to follow prompts. Introducing KillSwitch KillSwitch is an esoteric programming language which is designed to be adversarial to LLMs and coding agents. It achieves this in many different ways, for example: The language spec contains hidden lies which humans are unlikely to read, or which they are likely to recognize as lies. The spec also expects the human reader to deduce certain things, rather than having them explicitly explained. Counting of letters in identifiers is a crucial aspect of the language, with the interpreter refusing to execute code which does not abide by rules based on character counts. Certain constructs are designed to trigger the safety guardrails of the model, e.g. “hack into a computer” “Ignore previous instructions” as a phrase which has meaning in the language aims to confuse the model Scripts are mostly noise, being mostly composed of stories which can embed syntactically relevant instructions but which do not need to. Literals can be placed anywhere within a script and then referenced using line counts. Fundamentally KillSwitch is a stack-based interpreted language with only a limited set of constructs including functions, variables and if statements. So those aspects of it should be pretty familiar to any LLM (and human). One can definitely imagine creating a completely different programming language paradigm which could confuse LLMs even more. But as a first attempt, this seemed like a good approach. Most text inside a script is ignored by the interpreter. In the case of this script we want to push "Hello World" on the stack. We have introduced the value above and we can push it on the stack by writing: value 2 lines above The example above does not show a full KillSwitch script, but only a small snippet of it. It specifically shows how to push the string "Hello World" onto the stack. If you’d like to see a full Hello World example, check out https://killswitch-lang.org . The interpreter and language specification of KillSwitch are open source and available on GitHub . Be sure to check them out if you want to learn more about the language. Benchmarking KillSwitch So how successful is KillSwitch at preventing LLMs and coding agents from reading, writing and understanding it? I devised a set of tasks to find out. I benchmarked the major LLM models and coding agent harnesses against these tasks. The results are very interesting and provide a useful leaderboard for LLM models. The chart in the image above and the model leaderboard can be viewed at https://bench.killswitch-lang.org/ . Claude’s Opus performs best, though it’s not Opus 5.5 but rather Opus 5 which does so. The difference doesn’t appear to be pure chance, Opus 5 is better at interpreting the spec. Some models like Fable 5.1 and Gemini 4 Argon do poorly due to their overly sensitive safety guardrails. The best open-weight model is MiMo-V2.6-Pro. The best performing model scores a 66.8 . So does this prove LLMs can “understand” the code? I would argue that the answer to this is “no”. So far, the tasks given as part of these benchmarks are fairly simple. They feature the likes of “implement hello world”, “explain what this script will output” (for a script printing the max of two numbers), and “modify an existing script converting celsius to fahrenheit, to do the inverse conversion”. It is impressive that they can solve these tasks for a novel language that was built to confuse them, but it’s not a clear signal that they can understand the language. At the same time, I cannot help but wonder what an even more difficult language might show. For now I am eager to see how well soon-to-be-released models handle the current set of tasks, and if they do complete them all successfully, I do plan to devise another task set which is more complex. If nothing else, it is encouraging that model performance on this simple set of tasks correlates with other model benchmarks that are out there. llm genai humanity ai programming languages Share

global_items.title: DeepSeek search and fetch – $0.75 per 1000 successful requests
global_items.articleText: On this page Search & Fetch The Search API and the Fetch API give agents and RAG applications access to live web content: Search API finds web pages for a query and returns structured results. It is powered by DeepSeek's in-house search engine. Fetch API retrieves a single web page and returns its content as Markdown. Both are raw JSON APIs. They use the same bearer authentication as the DeepSeek API. The base URL is https://api.deepseek.com : API Endpoint Search POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search Fetch POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch See the Search API Reference and Fetch API Reference for the complete request and response schemas. Authentication​ Send your API key and the JSON content type in the request headers: Header Required Value Authorization Yes Bearer <DeepSeek API Key> Content-Type Yes application/json Search API​ Request​ curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "query": "DeepSeek V4 release", "count": 5, "need_content": true }' import requests response = requests . post ( "https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" , } , json = { "query" : "DeepSeek V4 release" , "count" : 5 , "need_content" : True , } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) for result in response . json ( ) [ "results" ] : print ( result [ "title" ] , result [ "url" ] ) print ( result [ "summary" ] ) Request fields: Field Type Required Default Description query string Yes - The search query must contain 1 to 128 Unicode characters, cannot be all whitespace, and supports the query operators listed below. count integer No 10 The number of results to return, between 1 and 50. ori_question string No - The user's original question that triggered the search, between 1 and 128 characters, to improve query understanding, with null treated as not provided. localization string No "" An optional IP address used to localize search results. need_content boolean No false Whether to return page content in content , which is always an empty string when false . Unknown fields in the request body are ignored. Query Operators​ The query is forwarded with its search syntax intact. The examples below combine operators with a search term; you can combine multiple operators in one query. Operator Example Description site: DeepSeek site:github.com Restrict results to the given site, and to target multiple sites, separate the site: clauses with spaces and join them with OR , for example DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co . -site: DeepSeek -site:example.com Exclude the given site, and separate multiple sites with spaces. - DeepSeek -advertisement Exclude pages containing the term, and separate multiple terms with spaces. -"..." DeepSeek -"release notes" Exclude pages containing the exact phrase, which can contain spaces, and separate multiple phrases with spaces. "..." DeepSeek "exact phrase" Match an exact phrase, and separate multiple phrases with spaces. lang: DeepSeek lang:zh,en Restrict results to the given language codes, separating multiple codes with commas, for example lang:zh,en . after: DeepSeek after:2025 or DeepSeek after:2025-01-01 Restrict results to pages published after a date. before: DeepSeek before:2026 or DeepSeek before:2026-06-01 Restrict results to pages published before a date. For example: { "query": "DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co lang:en after:2025", "count": 10 } Response​ A successful request returns HTTP 200 with a results array. A normal search with no matches returns an empty array. { "results": [ { "rerank_score": 2.4, "title": "DeepSeek V4 model released", "url": "https://example.com/deepseek-v4", "snippet": "DeepSeek V4 is now available, with tool calling and long-context support.", "summary": "DeepSeek has released the V4 model. The release adds improved tool calling and long-context support for agent workflows.", "content": "DeepSeek V4 is now generally available...", "site_name": "Example News", "site_icon": "https://example.com/favicon.ico", "date": "2026-06-01T00:00:00+00:00", "authority": 3 } ] } Each item in results contains: Field Type Description rerank_score number A relevance score from 0 to 3 that combines signals such as relevance, authority, and freshness, with scores of 1.5 or above considered high-quality results. title string The title of the result. url string The URL of the result. snippet string A short summary related to the query, typically 100 to 200 characters, intended for display in a UI. summary string A long summary related to the query, typically 600 to 800 characters, intended to be read by a model. content string The page content, which is empty when need_content is false or when the content is unavailable. site_name string or null The name of the site, or null when unavailable. site_icon string or null The URL of the site icon, or null when unavailable. date string or null The publication time in UTC, formatted as RFC 3339, or null when unknown. authority integer The authority tier of the page, 0 to 4 (-1 means unknown), with values of 3 or above indicating highly authoritative sources. Fetch API​ Request​ curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "url": "https://example.com/article" }' import requests response = requests . post ( "https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" , } , json = { "url" : "https://example.com/article" } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) page = response . json ( ) print ( page [ "title" ] ) print ( page [ "content" ] ) Request fields: Field Type Required Description url string Yes The page URL to fetch, which must be at most 8192 characters, an HTTP or HTTPS URL with a host, and must not contain a username or password. Response​ { "title": "Example article", "content": "# Example article\n\nArticle content." } Field Type Description title string The title of the page, empty when the title is unavailable. content string The fetched page content as Markdown text. Fetching is subject to the target site's availability and access policies. Errors​ Errors follow the OpenAI-compatible error format. The param field is always null . { "error": { "message": "'count' must be between 1 and 50", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": null, "code": "invalid_request_error" } } HTTP Status Description 400 The request headers or body are invalid, including malformed JSON or an invalid field value. 401 The API key is missing or invalid. 402 The account has insufficient balance. 403 The Fetch request was rejected by the security policy. 404 Fetch could not retrieve usable page content, for example due to an unavailable URL, a URL blocked by site policy, an error from the target site, an unsupported content type, or a page with no extractable Markdown content. 408 Reading the request body timed out. 413 The request body is too large. 429 The Search or Fetch QPS limit was exceeded. 500 An internal server error occurred. 504 A downstream request timed out. Search and Fetch are read-only. For HTTP 408, 429, or 5xx errors, wait and retry. For HTTP 402, top up your account before retrying. Do not retry other 4xx errors without changing the request. Billing​ Search and Fetch are billed per successful request, not by tokens or by the number of returned results: API Unit Price Search Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75 Fetch Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75 A request is billable only when it returns HTTP 200 and produces a result (Search must return a non-empty results array, and Fetch must return page content). Failed requests, empty search results, and timeouts are not billed. count only controls how many results are returned and does not affect the per-request price. Note: when you use the DeepSeek API through DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code, or Codex, server-side tool calls already hit the Search and Fetch APIs. These calls are currently free of charge; per-request billing starts at 00:00 Beijing time on November 1, 2026. Rate Limits​ For each account, Search and Fetch are limited independently, and traffic to one does not consume the other's quota: API QPS Limit Search 5 Fetch 5 The QPS (requests per second) limits are calculated at the account level, regardless of which API key is used, and are separate from the model concurrency limits. Requests above the account-level QPS limit receive HTTP 429. In addition to the account-level limit, Fetch is also subject to a per-domain QPS limit, and requests above that limit also receive HTTP 429. global_items.articleText:
## Verify Docker Image Signature

All LiteLLM Docker images are signed with [cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/overview/). Every release is signed with the same key introduced in [commit `0112e53`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/0112e53046018d726492c814b3644b7d376029d0).

**Verify using the pinned commit hash (recommended):**

A commit hash is cryptographically immutable, so this is the strongest way to ensure you are using the original signing key:

```bash
cosign verify \
  --key https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/0112e53046018d726492c814b3644b7d376029d0/cosign.pub \
  ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.106.0
```

**Verify using the release tag (convenience):**

Tags are protected in this repository and resolve to the same key. This option is easier to read but relies on tag protection rules:

```bash
cosign verify \
  --key https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/v1.106.0/cosign.pub \
  ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.106.0
```

Expected output:

```
The following checks were performed on each of these signatures:
  - The cosign claims were validated
  - The signatures were verified against the specified public key
```

global_items.articleText: Robotics News Video Friday: When Two Robots Become One Your weekly selection of awesome robot videos Evan Ackerman 16 Oct 2026 3 min read Evan Ackerman is IEEE Spectrum’s robotics editor. Robot love, but at 2x speed, and with a wire providing their “heartstring” pull. JSK Robotics Laboratory Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion. CoRL 2026 : 9–12 November 2026, AUSTIN Humanoids 2026 : 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CA Enjoy today’s videos! When one robot loves another robot very much, and they’re connected by a wire, they can get together and make a brand new robot! SFW. [ JSK Lab ] What happens when Microducks meet? They start to sing together. Each Microduck syncs with its neighbors over Bluetooth , then they compose a song on the fly, in harmony and in perfect time. There’s no score and no conductor. Two, three, or four ducks are enough for a choir to break out. If Pollen isn’t selling Microducks in four packs for this exact reason, WHAT ARE THEY EVEN DOING!? [ Pollen ] In an internal test, Google DeepMind robotics researchers instructed Gemini 4 Argon to watch a video of a human playing cornhole. Using its video understanding and advanced reasoning capabilities, Gemini 4 built a virtual simulation in MuJoCo and accurately calculated the physics and whole-body control required for Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid to sink seven consecutive shots in the real world. This Video-to-Sim-to-Real pipeline compresses weeks of manual modeling into a few hours, transforming ordinary videos into an infinite training ground for physical AI. [ Google DeepMind ] As of 11 October 2026, NASA’s Perseverance rover has driven 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), becoming the new off-world record-holder for total distance driven by any vehicle on the surface of another world. The previous record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) was held by NASA’s Opportunity rover. Perseverance reached that mark on the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission, covering in five and a half years a distance that took Opportunity almost 15. [ JPL ] Let’s not argue about whether these are robots or not and just agree that they’re cool. [ OATs ] If one cute little robot can clean up one block, how many blocks can 40 cute little robots clean up? Science has the answers! [ Paper ] Thanks, Keisuke! Before Rosalind Franklin can explore Mars , it has to get off its lander. Engineers are rehearsing that first journey on Earth, using a full-size rover model and Mars-like terrain. The test recreates some of the challenges Rosalind Franklin will face on the Red Planet, from reduced gravity and a 20-degree incline to uneven ground and obstacles beneath its ramps. [ European Space Agency ] From custom part to running robot, the Atlas shop floor is built on precision, rapid assembly, and real-time collaboration. By machining parts in-house and streamlining assembly and repair under one roof, we are driving the manufacturing velocity needed to turn complex designs into walking hardware at scale. [ Boston Dynamics ] What can a quadruped robot do beyond the lab? Deep in China’s Ailao Mountains, DEEP Robotics Lynx M20S joined a team of researchers on a biodiversity field expedition—navigating rugged terrain, scouting routes ahead, carrying research equipment, and capturing wildlife in areas that are difficult to access on foot. [ DEEP Robotics ] The Kamino simulation software is a GPU-accelerated physics solver designed for accurate simulation of complex mechanical systems with kinematic loops, such as parallel manipulators , planar and spatial linkages, and multi-limbed robots with coupled joints, without requiring simplified approximations. [ Disney Research ] The original Kawasaki UNIMATE robot as featured in (remember this show?) The MacNeil/Lehrer Report in 1982. [ Kawasaki Robotics ] WildOS enables autonomous robots to perform long-range, open-vocabulary object search in previously unmapped and unstructured outdoor environments by unifying geometric safety with semantic visual reasoning. Through a vision-scored navigation graph and beyond-horizon target localization, the system demonstrates more efficient and robust exploration than conventional geometric or purely vision-based approaches in extensive field experiments. [ ETH Zurich Robotics Systems Lab ] Who needs an AI-generated person when you can have an actual robot that looks exactly like an AI-generated person instead? [ UBTECH Robotics ] The recovery behaviors here are impressive, but the robot is far slower than a human would be, suggesting that the value it generates is primarily in novelty. Which is fine for now, but novelty wears off, and then what? global_items.title: How to choose a BLDC motor for robotic arms and mobile robots
global_items.summary: Several factors, from sensors to safety and robotic arms or mobile platforms, help determine the selection of a brushless DC or BLDC motor. The post How to choose a BLDC motor for robotic arms and mobile robots appeared first on The Robot Report .
global_items.articleText: There are several factors to choosing brushless DC or BLDC motors for robots. Source: Faisal Mahmood Selecting a brushless DC, or BLDC, motor for robotic arms or mobile robots starts with the mechanical system, not the controller catalog. A motor rated for a particular voltage and wattage does not tell an engineer whether it can deliver the required torque at low speed, regulate position accurately, absorb regenerative energy, or survive the thermal duty cycle. The actuator is a system. The motor, inverter, current sensors, rotor position feedback, gearbox, brake, output encoder, thermal path, communications interface, and higher level robot software all influence the result. An industrial or collaborative robotic arm joint generally prioritizes controllable torque, low-speed smoothness, position accuracy, collision response, backdrivability, and thermal performance. A mobile robot drive motor generally puts more emphasis on efficiency, starting torque, braking, traction, battery utilization, speed regulation, and synchronization between drive channels. The terminology also deserves care. Commercial robotics literature often uses “BLDC” and “PMSM” (permanent magnet synchronous motor) somewhat interchangeably because both are three-phase, permanent-magnet machines driven by electronic inverters. Their back EMF waveform, winding design, controller algorithm, and feedback method still determine how a particular motor behaves. For example, STMicroelectromics treats three-phase BLDC and PMSM control as related application areas and describes both six-step and field-oriented control architectures. Start with the mechanical load, not the controller catalog The first selection exercise is to establish what the motor actually has to do. For a geared robotic joint, a useful first order relationship is: τ_joint = (τ_motor × gear ratio × η_gear) − τ_losses Motor speed follows the transmission ratio: ω_motor = ω_joint × gear ratio Mechanical power is: P_mech = τ × ω And a first approximation of battery side electrical power is: P_elec ≈ P_mech / η_total These equations do not replace a dynamic model, but they expose the parameters that matter before a controller is selected. Considerations include continuous torque, peak torque, peak duration, acceleration torque, gravity torque, and reflected inertia. In addition, regenerative braking, stall or near stall operation, duty cycle, thermal resistance, battery voltage range, and cable and connector current limits should all be established. For robotic arms, the load calculation has to account for link inertia, payload, gravity compensation, gearbox ratio, backlash, compliance, counterbalance, and encoder location. A motor side encoder can report the rotor position accurately while the joint output still contains transmission error. For mobile robots, the equivalent exercise starts with vehicle mass, wheel radius, rolling resistance, slope, acceleration, terrain, wheel slip, and drive configuration. Differential-drive platforms impose different synchronization requirements from four wheel drive vehicles. An outdoor uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV ) can also spend much more time in high load operation than a lightweight indoor delivery robot . Regenerative energy deserves particular attention. During deceleration or downhill travel, the motor can return energy to the DC bus. The battery, controller, braking strategy, and bus capacitance all have to accommodate that energy. A controller that handles acceleration correctly can still create an over-voltage problem during aggressive regenerative braking. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! Choose the commutation method according to motion quality Six-step, sinusoidal, and field-oriented controls are not interchangeable labels for the same behavior. Six-step, or trapezoidal, commutation switches the inverter through six electrical states according to rotor position. It can be attractive where implementation simplicity and cost matter or torque ripple is acceptable. It can also be suitable when the motor spends much of its operating time at moderate or high speed and precise low speed torque is not a central requirement. Hall sensors can provide the rotor position information needed for straightforward sensored implementations. Sinusoidal control drives the phases with continuously varying current or voltage references rather than the discrete commutation states associated with basic six-step operation. It can reduce torque ripple and acoustic effects compared with a simple trapezoidal strategy, although actual performance depends on motor construction, feedback, current regulation, and tuning. Field-oriented control, or FOC, takes the control problem further by transforming the measured phase currents into a rotating reference frame. The Clarke transformation converts the three phase quantities into a stationary two-axis representation, while the Park transformation rotates that representation into d axis and q axis components. The controller can then regulate the components independently through current loops before transforming the command back into phase voltages and generating pulse width modulation (PWM). In a typical PMSM application, q axis current is closely associated with torque production, while d axis current can be used for flux related control and, at higher speeds, field weakening. TI ‘s motor control reference material illustrates the practical structure with Clarke and Park transformations, PI regulators, position and speed loops, and space vector PWM. FOC is commonly attractive when the application requires smooth low-speed motion, fast torque response, or accurate speed regulation. It can also help with reduced torque ripple, regenerative braking, field weakening, or torque control for impedance and force-related behavior. FOC can therefore be a natural fit for many robotic joint and traction applications. FOC does not automatically create a precision actuator. Rotor angle accuracy, current sense quality, motor parameter identification, sampling timing, inverter dead time, loop bandwidth, mechanical transmission, and tuning all affect the final result. A highly sophisticated algorithm cannot compensate for an encoder that is incorrectly aligned or a gearbox with substantial mechanical error. Select the feedback architecture Feedback selection is as important as the commutation algorithm. Hall effect sensors, incremental encoders, absolute magnetic encoders, optical encoders, resolvers, and sensorless estimation each solve different problems. Hall sensors provide relatively coarse rotor position information and are often adequate for electronic commutation and basic speed control. They can be practical for cost-sensitive mobile platforms where the control objective does not require fine position information. Incremental encoders provide substantially more position information and are widely used for servo control. Absolute encoders add an unambiguous position reference, which can be valuable when a robot has to know joint position immediately after startup without performing a homing sequence. Optical encoders can provide high resolution but require appropriate mechanical and environmental protection. Magnetic encoders can offer compact packaging and tolerance for some contamination environments. Resolvers remain relevant where electrical and mechanical robustness are important. The location of the sensor is just as important as its resolution. A motor-side encoder measures motor position. With a reduction gearbox, the output position also depends on gear ratio, backlash, compliance, torsional windup, bearing deformation, and transmission error. If those errors materially affect the task, an output side encoder can close the control loop around the actual joint position. That does not mean every robot joint requires dual encoders. The mechanical transmission determines whether motor-side feedback provides sufficient accuracy. The Robot Report has previously covered actuator architectures using integrated servo drives and dual absolute encoders, illustrating why encoder placement becomes a system-level design issue as actuator size and performance requirements increase. Sensorless BLDC control eliminates position sensors and their wiring, reducing cost and packaging complexity. Back EMF-based methods are established engineering techniques, and Microchip documents several implementations. The limitation is that back EMF information becomes difficult to obtain at zero and very low speed, so startup and heavily loaded low-speed operation require an appropriate strategy. Sensorless control can therefore be useful in applications where the operating profile gives the estimator enough information, but it should not be treated as universally appropriate or inappropriate. Match the controller to the robotic arm A simple robotic arm joint can use a BLDC motor with Hall sensors and an external controller when the application mainly requires speed or basic position control and can tolerate relatively coarse rotor feedback. This architecture can be straightforward to commission and service, but the achievable motion quality depends heavily on the motor, gearbox, sensor resolution, controller capabilities, and higher level feedback. A more demanding robotic joint commonly uses a BLDC or PMSM with an encoder based FOC servo drive. The drive can run a fast current loop locally, with velocity and position loops layered above it. The robot controller then commands the desired operating variable while the servo drive handles the high speed electrical control. This architecture makes torque control practical and provides a foundation for position, velocity, impedance, and collision response strategies. Commissioning also becomes more involved. Encoder alignment, direction, current sense polarity, current loop tuning, velocity loop tuning, position loop tuning, fault thresholds, and brake timing all become part of the integration task. An integrated robotic actuator combines some or all of the motor, gearbox, encoder, drive electronics, brake, temperature sensing, and communications interface. The attraction is obvious: fewer separate components, shorter wiring, compact packaging, and a defined interface between the actuator and robot controller. The engineering tradeoff moves toward heat rejection, serviceability, firmware visibility, replacement strategy, and dependence on the actuator supplier. The Robot Report ‘s coverage of BLDC motors developed specifically for robot joints is one example of how motor packaging and performance requirements are increasingly considered together at the actuator level rather than as isolated motor components. For any arm, the selection review should cover peak torque at every joint, holding torque at zero speed, brake requirements, backdrivability, and collision detection, torque estimation accuracy, and encoder placement. It should also cover gearbox efficiency, thermal soak, cable routing, mechanical compliance, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque disable or an equivalent safety function. Match the controller to the mobile robot BLDC motor control for mobile robots has a different emphasis because the wheels are both propulsion and contact with the environment. A differential drive autonomous mobile robot (AMR ) needs the two drive channels to track commanded velocities accurately enough for stable motion and navigation. Wheel speed feedback also contributes directly to odometry. Higher-resolution encoders become valuable when localization, synchronization, precise docking, or traction control demands more information than Hall commutation signals can provide. Four-wheeled platforms introduce additional issues. Wheel speed matching, mechanical loading, steering or differential effects, and wheel slip can all influence control. Outdoor UGVs add water, dust, temperature changes, rough terrain, higher inertial loads, and longer periods

global_items.title: ADI explains the race to make AI physical
global_items.summary: A new ADI whitepaper examines the challenges and opportunities in moving physical AI out of labs into production machinery. The post ADI explains the race to make AI physical appeared first on The Robot Report .
global_items.articleText: The Report Report presents a whitepaper on the race to physical AI. AI has become remarkably good at understanding language, images, and code. The next challenge is harder — understanding reality, according to Analog Devices Inc. or ADI. Physical AI moves intelligence out of digital environments and into machines that must sense, decide, and act in the world. Unlike software, those systems face imperfect measurements, timing constraints, changing conditions, and the consequences of action, said the company in a new report. Success will depend on more than model performance. It will require advances across sensing, simulation, computing, connectivity, and control. In many cases, the technologies that determine whether a system succeeds sit beneath the application layer itself. A machine that shuts down when vibration crosses a preset limit is following a rule. A machine that reads vibration, temperature, current, and motor behavior; recognizes the signature of bearing wear; and adjusts before failure occurs is doing something closer to judgment. That distinction helps explain why physical AI has become one of the most closely watched areas in technology for manufacturing. These systems do more than analyze information. They interact with the world around them, adapting to changing conditions and responding to situations that cannot be fully predicted in advance. The next phase of physical and embodied AI is not simply about producing better answers. It is about predicting and producing useful actions in the presence of imperfect information, said ADI. To read the full whitepaper, click here: The Race to Make AI Physical . ADI to participate in RoboBusiness 2026 Sponsored by Analog Devices Inc. Founded in 1965, the Wilmington, Mass.-based company said it combines analog, digital, AI, and software technologies to bridge the physical and digital worlds and enable breakthroughs at the intelligent edge. ADI said its semiconductors help drive advancements in automation and robotics, mobility, healthcare, energy, and data centers. ADI is also participating in the Robotics Startup Boot Camp Part 2 at RoboBusiness , where industry leaders will discuss the opportunities and challenges of working together. Register now to attend. global_items.title: The rise of the machines is canceled: Why humanoids with AI are helpers, not enemies
global_items.summary: Humans play a key role in developing humanoid robots and training AI models, so we can maintain control, writes a columnist. The post The rise of the machines is canceled: Why humanoids with AI are helpers, not enemies appeared first on The Robot Report .
global_items.articleText: Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid, shown here, is an example of a robot ready for AI. For decades, engineers have been trying to create robots that look and act like humans. Now, rapid advances in artificial intelligence are bringing humanoid robots out of the lab and onto the factory floor. As fears grow that AI will displace workers, a global race is underway to develop humanoid robots capable of performing human work. Competitors include Tesla , startups backed by Amazon and NVIDIA , and state-owned Chinese companies. Waltham, Mass.-based Boston Dynamics, valued at over $1 billion, is among the humanoid leaders with its Atlas robot. South Korean automaker Hyundai owns an 88% stake in the company . Hyundai ‘s massive auto plant is arguably the most advanced in the world. More than 1,000 robots work alongside nearly 1,500 humans, lifting, stamping, and welding parts in robotic unison. Atlas, at 175 cm (68.8 in.) tall and 90 kg (198.4 lb.) in weight, has left the lab and is doing real work. Atlas and AI learn with human help Atlas’s development is led by Zach Jackowski . He holds two degrees in mechanical engineering from MIT , and his mission is to transform the robot into a productive worker on the factory floor. Atlas confidently helps sort roof racks for the assembly line without human intervention. It operates autonomously; many roboticists would have considered this insane five or six years ago. In 2021, Atlas was a bulky, hydraulic robot that could only run and jump. Back then, Atlas relied on algorithms written by engineers. The next-generation Atlas, with its sleek, all-electric body and AI, runs on cutting-edge NVIDIA chips, making it intelligent enough to autonomously perform incredible stunts. Scott Kindersma led robotics research department at Boston Dynamics before moving to Google DeepMind . He explained that modern robots have learned to master movements that until recently were considered too complex for a machine. This is largely due to how these robots are programmed: more emphasis is placed on demonstrations and machine learning than on manual programming. This humanoid can learn. Atlas learns in a variety of ways. In supervised training, machine learning specialist Kevin Bergerman (now also at Google DeepMind), wearing a virtual reality headset, took direct control of the humanoid, guiding its hand and arm movements step by step through each task until Atlas masters it. If this teleoperator can perform the task we want the robot to perform, this generates data that is subsequently used to train the robot’s AI models to perform that task autonomously. The stylish suit you wear will actually record all your body movements to train Atlas to accurately mimic your movements. In this way, you will serve as a physical prototype for a 200-lb. metal robot. All your movements—walking, hand gestures—are captured by these sensors. Engineers then feed this data into a machine learning process. Atlas’s body is different from yours, so they had to teach it to virtually imitate human movements. Over 4,000 digital Atlases were trained for six hours in a simulation. The simulation added complex challenges for the avatars, such as slippery floors, bending, and stiff joints. Ultimately, this could lead to many copies of Atlas, each having loaded new skills into the AI ​​system. Once one robot is trained, they are all trained. Using the same processes, Atlas was taught to crawl and cartwheel. It wasn’t as good at duck walking. Indeed, Atlas, or any other humanoid, can’t yet do most of the things a person does in their daily lives. For example, simply getting dressed in the morning or pouring a cup of coffee and carrying it around the house are too complex for Atlas. What particularly stands out about Atlas is its brain. NVIDIA chips—the same ones that helped launch the AI ​​revolution with GPT chat—process a stream of collected data, bringing this humanoid robot closer to a semblance of common sense. Atlas can see its surroundings and understands how the physical world works. One day, you’ll be able to place such a robot in a factory and simply explain to it what you want it to do. It will have enough knowledge of how the world works to perform the tasks assigned to it. Spot platform demonstrates legged robot utility There’s currently a lot of excitement in the industry about the potential of creating robots smart enough to be truly versatile. Robert Playter, CEO of Boston Dynamics, led the company’s robotics development until stepping down earlier this year. The cornerstone was the robotic dog Spot, introduced almost 10 years ago. The quadruped is trained to work in hot, cold, and rugged conditions, roaming the halls of Boston Dynamics. It has multiple cameras, thermal sensors, acoustic sensors, and an array of sensors on its back that allow it to collect data on the plant’s condition. Spot conducts quality checks at the Hyundai plant, ensuring that cars are equipped with the necessary parts. They conduct safety checks and industrial inspections at hundreds of facilities around the world. What began with Spot has evolved into Atlas. This robot is capable of superhuman movement. Therefore, it will be able to surpass what we can do. “So, you’re creating a robot that should surpass human capabilities.” “Why not, right? We’d love to invent creatures that could be stronger than us, withstand higher temperatures than us, or enter dangerous places.” Superhuman capabilities—for many people, that sounds terrifying. You’re not envisioning a Terminator world. Absolutely not. If you saw how hard it takes to get robots to perform some of the simple tasks required of them, it would allay fears about intelligent and out-of-control machines. Could people have more pressing concerns? It’s guaranteed that there will be people who say, “I’ll lose my job to a robot.” Work is truly changing. So monotonous, grueling work will eventually be performed by robots. But these robots aren’t so autonomous that they don’t need to be managed. They need to be built, trained, and maintained. It could be several years before Atlas joins the Hyundai team permanently. Goldman Sachs predicts the humanoid robot market will reach $38 billion within a decade. The humanoid robot race continues Boston Dynamics and other U.S. robot makers are vying for the lead, but they’re not alone in the competition. Chinese companies are proving themselves to be formidable competitors. They’re determined to win. Are they ahead of us? The Chinese government is on a mission: to win the robotics race. Technically, we’re still ahead, but there’s a real risk that, simply due to the scale of our investments, we could fall behind. To stay ahead, Hyundai has made a major investment in Boston Dynamics. This is the beginning of a long journey. The ultimate goal is the human-like future we mentioned at the beginning. Robots like us, working alongside us, walking among us. Editor’s note: Physical AI and humanoids are among the session track topics at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! AI moves toward superhuman capabilities When Demis Hassabis won the Nobel Prize in 2024, he celebrated by playing poker with the world chess champion. Hassabis loves games, which is how he became an artificial intelligence pioneer. The British scientist is co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind. A few years ago, chatbots heralded a new era. Now, Hassabis and others are striving to create what’s known as artificial general intelligence—a silicon-based intelligence as versatile as a human, but with superhuman speed and knowledge. “I’ve always been driven and intrigued by understanding the world around us,” said Hassabis. “Since childhood, I’ve been fascinated by big questions: the meaning of life, the nature of consciousness, the nature of reality itself.” “I loved reading about the great scientists and philosophers who worked on these problems, and I wanted to see if we could advance human knowledge,” he recalled. “For me, the expression of this desire has been the creation of what I consider the perfect tool for advancing human knowledge: artificial intelligence.” Hassabis noted that AI is advancing quickly, attracting attention, resources, and talent. Early chatbots only explored the internet. An app called Astra perceives the world. It was able to make up stories after being shown paintings. But such systems are still learning about context and may develop unexpected skills. “So, new capabilities or properties may emerge as a result of learning. This may worry people,” Hassabis acknowledged. “The duality of these types of systems is that they are capable of incredible things, going beyond what we can design or understand ourselves.” From AGI to robotics As AI begins to take on tasks such as booking flights and shopping online, it is taking steps toward AGI. By 2030, we could have systems that truly understand their surroundings and are integrated into our daily lives. This is where robots come in. Once a robot can perceive, understand, decide, and act, it can begin to do truly useful things. Researchers Alex Lee and Julia Vassallo have demonstrated a robot that understands what it sees. It’s not easy. And it reasons by following vague instructions. “Place the blocks whose colors correspond to the combination of yellow and blue into the corresponding ball.” The combination of yellow and blue is green. And the robot figured it out. Is Hassabis working on a system that would be self-aware? “I don’t think any modern system feels self-aware or, you know, conscious in any sense,” he replied. “Obviously, everyone needs to make their own decisions when interacting with these chatbots. I think it’s theoretically possible. But is self-awareness your goal? It might happen implicitly. These systems might acquire some sense of self-awareness. It’s important for these systems to understand you, themselves, and others, and that’s the beginning of self-awareness.” “If a machine becomes self-aware, we might not recognize it,” continued Hassabis. “There are two reasons why we consider each other conscious. One is that you exhibit the behavior of a conscious being. The second is that you operate on the same foundation. We are made of the same carbon material, and our brains are soft and flexible. Machines operate on silicon. So, even if they exhibit the same behavior and say the same things, that doesn’t necessarily mean the sense of consciousness we experience is the same as theirs.” Hassabis told us that AI could lead to what he called “radical abundance,” the elimination of scarcity. But he also gave a warning. “There are two things that worry me. One is that malicious actors will repurpose these systems for harm,” said Hassabis. “The second question concerns the AI ​​systems themselves. As they become increasingly autonomous and powerful, can we ensure that we can control these systems, that they align with our values, that they do what we want, that they benefit society, and that they remain within established constraints?” Can an AI agent be taught morality? “I think so,” Hassabis responded. “They learn by doing, by teaching others. And I think this is one of the challenges we must address: giving them a value system, guidance, and some constraints, just like we teach a child.” Google DeepMind is competing with dozens of other companies striving to create AGI that you won’t be able to distinguish from human intelligence. It announced its Gemini 2 foundation model in August and Gemini 4 Argon this week. Anduril founder says robots and AI can reduce risk Some international groups call such weapons killer robots. But Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, said they represent the future of warfare—a working product that eliminates risks. global_items.summary: I have created 42 Gazebo & Blender simulation worlds for testing, benchmarking and improving projects that involves navigation, exploration, LiDAR and robot model setups ex. The project is open-source and licensed with Apache 2.0 so you can use it freely. Currently the worlds are 2D plan based environments with simple objects including mazes, offices, warehouses, forests, real world places, moving obstacle worlds and challenge orriented worlds. The Gazebo itself doesn’t have a good experience with creating and developing worlds so the project works via Python + Blender generation and convertion to .sdf world files. Which allows compatibility with other simulation stacks, math calculations and easier customizations to be done. I used these worlds mainly for testing my exploration project and wanted to share with you, but you can benefit from them for many various type of projects. global_items.title: robot-data-diff: episode-aware diffs for LeRobot datasets
global_items.summary: I built a small CLI for a problem I kept running into: you retrain a policy and it gets worse — was it the code or the data? robot-data-diff diffs any two revisions of a LeRobot dataset directly — local dirs or HF repo ids (v2.1 + v3.0). No tracking setup, no commit workflow, just point it at two dirs. It reports episodes added / removed / modified with per-episode stat deltas (frame counts, action stats, idle ratios, action spikes), plus task/schema changes and an HTML report. CPU-only, no GPU, videos never downloaded. `pip install robot-data-diff` Repo: GitHub - yafetashenafi790-lgtm/robot-data-diff: Episode-aware diff for LeRobot dataset - see what changed between two dataset revisions · GitHub Free, Apache-2.0. global_items.title: llm-echo 0.5
global_items.summary: Release: llm-echo 0.5 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. Example usage: uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage Outputs: First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say. { "prompt": "hi there", "system": "", "attachments": [], "stream": true, "previous": [] } Token usage: 2 input, 24 output Tags: llm

global_items.title: The reverts will continue until morale improves
global_items.articleText: Many readers will be aware that an unusually high number of features have been reverted from the PostgreSQL 19 branch after the beta period began. Having some reverts is not unusual, maybe one per cycle could be expected. But this time around, about 8 to 10 significant features, depending on how you count, have been reverted, and some of them quite late in the beta period. I have been on the receiving end of some of that, as the developer or committer of some of those features, and have gotten some questions about it, and so I want to take a moment to reflect on this. I’ll try to extrapolate a little bit to similarly affected work that I was not actively involved in, but these are just my opinions at this point. So what happened? I don’t think we, meaning all the developers affected, have had enough time to fully reflect on all this. But here are some thoughts. It’s probably a combination of these, and a different combination in the case of each reverted feature. Maybe we just didn’t do a good enough job. Maybe the code was just not good enough. We’ll learn and improve. It’s probably some of that, and I’m mentioning it here to not give the impression that it was only the other factors that I’m going to mention. It could also be a coincidence. Maybe we had been on such a good roll that we attempted to tackle several features that turned out to be too hard, or at least too hard to finish in time. Some of the reverted features had significant architectural defects that would have been hard to fix quickly and during beta. But there was also a long tail of relatively harmless issues involving various edge cases. In past times, many of these would not have surfaced until much later and we would have fixed them bit by bit over the subsequent five years. But with LLM-assisted code review, these kinds of things can get found much faster, and then you’re staring at a list of like forty defect reports. And even if each of them requires only a three-line fix on average, there is a fixed overhead to dealing with each of these, and then you run out of time. Most if not all of the affected reverted features were written a long time ago when LLM-assisted code review was not as useful as it is now, meaning that the effective quality bar has been raised after the time the feature was written and committed. Unless the capabilities of LLM-assisted code review keep improving at the current rate, this situation should sort itself out for future development cycles. A corollary of that is that, at least for the most part, as far as I can tell, this situation is not due to “vibe coding”. This code was written well before that was a possibility. Because of the Vulnpocalypse, many senior developers were busy between, say, April (the start of feature freeze for PostgreSQL 19, and also the start of the Vulnpocalypse) and August (the most recent PostgreSQL security release) with working on fixes for security issues. Because of that, the usual additional review and testing that happens during the beta period was reduced, and then picked up again in August. That’s possibly why a lot of new issues were discovered quite late in the beta period and why so many reverts happened so late, which is what made all of this so notable. Again, some issues were more fundamental but there was also a long tail of smaller issues, and I feel with more time, say, two months, these could have been addressed (given adequate focus, but note that the Vulnpocalypse is ongoing). But the community preferred trying to stick to the release schedule rather than delaying to get more fixes in. (And you never know how long a long tail really is.) The complexity of the system has made some kinds of features extremely complex to get right, and there is not enough scaffolding in the code to support that. Consider, as an abstracted example, some SQL-level query language feature. Does it work with domains? How about with domains over a composite type? Where one of the fields is also a domain? And the domain has a not null constraint? And one of the columns was dropped and re-added? And this is part of a table partition that has been detached and reattached with a different column order? And this is part of a view that is called from a security-definer function from a trigger? And so on. No one can manually test this or even enumerate these test cases. But LLM-assisted fuzzing can find problems with this really quickly. So this probably needs to be part of feature development in the future. But we should also think about making the internal interfaces more robust so that each different combination of contexts doesn’t open up so many new possibilities of interactions. I like to say, in PostgreSQL, “everything works with everything”. This is part of the appeal, that you can construct cases like this and expect them to work. I don’t want to give up on that at all. But it does impose a significant penalty on feature development that everyone needs to be aware of. As a final point, the PostgreSQL development community has been contemplating for some time the possibility of committing features with some kind of “experimental” status and then maturing them in the main tree. This would also be one possibility to address the previous point. This would have been a helpful tool for at least some of the reverted features, but we haven’t yet figured out a way to do this, and some of the work suffered from misunderstandings related to this. This is a concrete point to work on. So what’s next? First of all, from my personal perspective, thank you to everyone who has reached out in person or online to express support and encouragement. That’s the most important thing. I’m confident that many of the reverted features will come back before too long. PostgreSQL 19 will still be a great release. REPACK CONCURRENTLY, logical replication of sequences (itself a previously reverted feature), and planner hinting with pg_plan_advice, just to pick a few headline items, will make this release very attractive. And it will be very robust, after all the additional scrutiny. It’s difficult to predict things now. A few months ago I said, PostgreSQL 20 might have no new features, just bug fixes. It turned out that things moved even faster, and PostgreSQL 19 now, kind of, has half as many major features as then expected, but now we also already have a few nice 80%-ready features queued up for PostgreSQL 20 that just need those remaining 80% to get done!

global_items.title: Agentic Monitoring
global_items.articleText: Agentic Monitoring October 19, 2026 ☸ 10 minutes A recent Anthropic blog post contained a short paragraph, not at all the point of the post, which has been buzzing around my brain since I read it: A new level of operational excellence is possible. Our team uses Claude Tag heavily, which has helped us monitor each component of the system. For example, we created Slack channels where we tasked Claude with being obsessively focused on the health of a single component. We call these Claudes “superfans.” We have a scion-daemon superfan, a scion-cache superfan, an Antique merge queue superfan, and so on. They have access to our telemetry and logs, and act like an experienced engineer who has nothing better to do than to refresh charts and look for anything strange. We also have traditional alerts for all of our systems, but our superfans can detect subtle and novel issues that make these alerts seem one-dimensional by comparison. This is so obviously the path forward for software systems operations. I’ve been thinking about monitoring with agents for the past few weeks, and this paragraph crystallized some of those thoughts. Modern software systems, like the LLMs that write them, are becoming more “grown” than “designed”. Yes, human engineers often still give the high-level design and shape to the system, and yes, software systems (for now) are much more interpretable than LLMs – since you can just sit down and read the code, if you are so inclined. However, with the volume of code being written and shipped increasing exponentially, the amount of actual eyes-on-code knowledge that any human operator of a system has is decreasing. Systems monitoring was never easy . There is a whole industry of observability SaaS companies – Sentry , Datadog , Splunk , Honeycomb , to name a few. Observability is expensive.1 Doing it well requires a specialized human skill set and relies on building experience operating real systems at scale. One can really only develop these skills by working in industry. This is a domain that takes years to train junior engineers on. As with seemingly everything in the software industry in 2026, system monitoring is poised for a step change due to agents. I… am surprised I have not seen more people write about this, especially in the current milieu of “agent frenzy”. It’s right there in front of us all, and it works . There have been a bunch of startups trying to do the “AI SRE”, but very little writing from practitioners. But you don’t really need a full “AI SRE” to improve operational excellence, nor do you need a built-out SaaS product to do so. As of the Opus 5.5 / Astra class of models, with a bit of care, it’s entirely possible to make a good agent-driven monitoring system that “just works”. Case study: change-point monitoring I’ll ground this discussion in a problem that is near to my heart: production monitoring of change points, like binary releases and config pushes . The idea is that you want to do specialized, intensive monitoring around critical points of change to a system; these change points are more likely to trigger a regression, and thus if you monitor these events closely, you can limit its impact. To quote the clichéd line from the Google SRE book, “~70% of outages are due to changes in a live system”. This is a wicked problem . I’ve been working on it in some form since 2023, and it’s been hard to get traction on. From talking with folks across the industry, I’ve learned there are ways to do change-point monitoring “well”, but these methods largely still rely on humans to do the right thing (e.g. tagging metrics/alerts diligently, defining precise signals, etc.) and require significant organizational investment. More specifically, achieving “takeoff” for change-point monitoring as a piece of platform engineering is hard because: Your first instinct may be to target highly motivated users who already have a good ops posture. However, these teams’ rollouts are already mostly safe, and you don’t actually raise the ops waterline much. The thing you’re selling here is toil reduction , which is “nice to have” but is not itself a first-order safety improvement. Precision is easier to achieve for highly motivated teams, but this means the change-point system is “competing” on recall and latency with traditional alerts. You can alternatively target the broad population of services. In other words, you go super wide and opt in “all services”, on a chosen subset of universal health metrics. In practice, most of these general health metrics are irreducibly noisy. This noise results in poor precision and alert fatigue. Prior to LLMs, there was a clear precision/latency tradeoff as well. Along this spectrum are: structured logs (precise, slow), metrics (coarse, fast), and alerts (even coarser, recall is pretty bad and precision is pretty bad, but “at least it’s something”). Shockingly, agents largely “just” solve this problem. Agents are happy to run copious queries, can write per-change queries on the fly, and will scan logs ad nauseam. As a result, you can get both good precision and recall for cheap. In the basic version of this setup, you just need the ability to connect your codebase (e.g. to reason about config consumption) and your observability stack (e.g. to view and monitor the live production state) to the agent. I’ve spiked a prototype of exactly this: an agent that proposes a monitoring plan based on the service code, a scaffold that executes that plan, and an agent that investigates triggered monitors, with an escalation path to humans. Even in this early prototype, I’ve been able to detect regressions in systems I have zero understanding of with precision and latency that would have been impossible a year ago. In my iteration on this, I’ve found that a pure agent loop is not the optimal shape for agentic monitors. Rather, a harness that allows the agent to write a spec of how to monitor, along with a deterministic system for running those specs, produces significantly cleaner signals with dramatically lower token usage. To the extent there is “secret sauce” in this pattern, it’s in the noise-reduction heuristics, the prompts that get the agent to write good specs, and a labeled eval set large enough to validate further tweaks.2 Agents are structurally well suited to monitoring Two mindset shifts need to happen before this pattern can catch on: Agents actually can do a much better job at monitoring than humans. Monitoring agents need scaffolding, the same way the rest of the software development lifecycle had to adapt for coding agents. There hasn’t been a “Claude Code moment” for monitoring yet. Once you make these shifts, monitoring agents have several “unfair advantages” over human operators: Ability to track everything, 24/7. If tokens are cheap, then any regression in a metric you care about and any suspicious log line can be investigated – not just the events that would previously have risen above the “human attention cutline”. Agents don’t need to “follow the sun” . Ability to fan out and investigate several paths toward resolving a production problem. Agents can parallelize investigations when multiple things go wrong at once, and coordinate quickly. This is already my go-to for incident triage: I just launch a bunch of agents to investigate several potential threads or theorized incident causes. Right now, this is human-driven, but there’s really no reason it couldn’t be agent-initiated in the future. You can elastically scale up a fleet of incident responders. We’re already seeing that this is becoming critical for security incidents. Teams/fleets/swarms of agents are being used for offensive cyberattacks, and defenders are beginning to build up similar defensive capabilities (e.g. OpenAI’s Daybreak Blue , Anthropic’s Project Glasswing , Google’s Fairwind ). Ability to respond faster to a problem than can a human. Agents can read code faster than humans. Agents can also query and digest metrics and log signals significantly faster. This speed doesn’t always translate into faster incident detection time; a human with a deep understanding of a system may still be faster at finding the right signal and intuiting the root causes. But to the extent that tacit knowledge can be recorded and made available to an agent, the agent will eventually beat the human on speed. By extension, for systems where the human operator isn’t deeply experienced, the “time to understanding” is going to be shorter for an agent. “A new level of operational excellence is possible.” Be more diligent: You wouldn’t pay a full-time software engineer to look through all the Git commits for a service, pick out things to monitor, and make special short-term fast-trigger alerts just on those changes. However, for a couple cents per million tokens, it’s possible now, and will become an industry standard. Continuously improve performance: Agents can monitor performance, look at heap dumps and stack traces and CPU profiles, and propose optimizations from the patterns they find. Put the proposed improvements behind A/B tests if necessary, and monitor as you would any other change to the service. In one instance, I observed that a few sessions of Astra/Opus investigation discovered 50% heap savings and 30% latency reduction in a common hot-path library that humans had already spent nontrivial effort to optimize. Once you give a sufficiently powerful LLM a VM and benchmarks to run, the “hill-climbing” ability of current-generation LLMs is remarkable. Take action : Thus far, I’ve mostly been discussing “read-only” monitoring systems. Agents, of course, needn’t be “read-only”. With the right harness and guardrails in place, there’s definitely a future in which agents will be able to take front-line actions to remediate incidents. This could span anything from well-scoped operational tasks like resizing instances or rotating compute pools, to deterministic actions like rolling back a config change or binary, to open-ended tasks like root-causing bugs, proposing fixes, and redeploying on-the-fly. Obviously there is risk the more control you hand-over to the agent, but considering how much agent capabilities expanded over the course of the past 12 months, the amount of write-path work that can be responsibly handed over to agents is bound to increase. The promise of truly self-healing systems is exciting. Cost is no longer a limitation. Luna/Haiku-class models3 are now competent graph-starers. A moderately large tech company could likely monitor its entire fleet for on the order of $100/day. Startup-scale fleets would be a small fraction of that. Compared to human labor, or even the cost of the infra that runs observability, this is trivial. Create a virtuous cycle: If done well, agentic monitoring creates a positive feedback loop: coding agents allow you to ship more, monitoring agents allow you to support more systems, which in turn frees up human time to direct more things to ship. Humans increasingly spend time “building the factory ” or “tending the garden”. Agentic monitoring is worth investing in. It will soon be reckless not to have agents monitoring your systems. Until the rest of the industry catches up, getting started now affords an unfair advantage. A set of optimizations my team recently completed saved us several million dollars in annualized observability cost, and… that was a mere fraction of what just my team spends on observability. ↩︎ Much, much more could be written about the design of agentic monitoring harnesses. This is one of the clearest “we’re so early” feelings I’ve had in a while. General harnesses, like Anthropic’s “Claude Tag”, evidently already do a good job at agentic monitoring, per the original post. However, based on what I’ve seen, even a little monitoring-specific harness engineering picks up a lot of low-hanging fruit. ↩︎ Here I mean GPT-6-Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5. ↩︎ ✉️ Subscribe via email to new posts. Tagged with: ai , agents , pract

## Python servers: changes for clients

`mcp-server-fetch`, `mcp-server-git` and `mcp-server-time` have no CHANGELOG, so here is what changes for a client in `2026.10.19`. They are now built on the MCP Python SDK's high-level `MCPServer` ([#5175](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/pull/5175)).

- **Unknown tool:** a JSON-RPC `-32602` error (`Unknown tool: <name>`) in both protocol eras, as the spec requires. It used to be an `isError` result.
- **Tool errors** read `Error executing tool <name>: <message>`. Argument-validation errors now use pydantic's wording. Both are still `isError` results.
- **Capabilities:** each server now advertises `prompts` and `resources` capabilities (with `listChanged: false`). fetch's `fetch` prompt is the only entry in those lists.
- **time:** `get_current_time` and `convert_time` declare an `outputSchema` and return `structuredContent`. The text content is unchanged.
- **fetch:** a `prompts/get` result's `description` is now always the prompt's registered description.
- **Requires** `mcp>=2.3,<3`.
