global_items.articleText: Robotics Magazine Feature Humanoid Robots The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build Agility Robotics’ first practical robotic worker is nothing like I dreamed Jonathan W. Hurst 8h 13 min read Vertical Author and Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst next to his new Digit 5 humanoid robot worker. Christie Hemm Klok Agility Robotics , the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5 . It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do. Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined. From ATRIAS to Digit My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals. We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS —short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait. With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be? Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones , and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie . Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard , Caltech , the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them. ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year. Agility Robotics Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion : A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash. Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1 , which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers. Why Digit Began With Warehouse Bins As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers. After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins . Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation . Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills. In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company , we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO . In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine. Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could. I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact. Turning Digit Into a Product I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary. Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities. While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction. Christie Hemm Klok I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move. Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned. Digit 5 Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements. Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can. global_items.title: Daimon Robotics building the infrastructure layer for tactile intelligence
global_items.summary: The company is connecting tactile sensing, real-world data collection, simulation, and AI models to help robots perform physical tasks more reliably. The post Daimon Robotics building the infrastructure layer for tactile intelligence appeared first on The Robot Report .
global_items.articleText: Credit: Daimon Robotics Vision has become central to modern robotics, but cameras alone cannot tell a robot everything it needs to know about physical contact. When handling flexible objects, inserting components, or manipulating delicate items, robots need information about forces, slippage, and contact that visual systems may miss. Daimon Robotics wants to provide the infrastructure to help robots develop that capability. Rather than focusing exclusively on tactile sensors or developing a single foundation model, the company is building a pipeline that connects tactile sensing, data collection, simulation, and AI models. Its goal is to turn physical interactions into useful training data that helps robots perform manipulation tasks more reliably. “By building tactile intelligence, we’re actually playing the role as an infrastructure provider,” Daimon’s Partner & VP of Technology Dr. Zhu told The Robot Report . “We’re not aiming to be a foundation model developer. We are providing the infrastructure for doing so for those downstream customers.” That distinction is central to Daimon’s strategy: develop the tools and data infrastructure that other companies can use to build more capable robotic systems. Building a pipeline for tactile data Collecting useful tactile data at scale presents a challenge. Unlike visual data, which can be captured relatively easily with cameras, tactile data depends on physical contact. The resulting information varies with an object’s material, geometry, the forces applied, and the task being performed. Daimon is developing a pipeline to capture and process these interactions, with tactile feedback operating at 30 Hz. The company is also working to connect real-world data with simulation, allowing physical interactions to inform training in virtual environments. The sim-to-real gap remains a significant challenge, particularly when accurately reproducing physical properties such as friction and contact forces. Daimon’s approach starts by calibrating simulations against real-world measurements before transferring collected data into simulated environments. “Let’s be frank; it’s not good enough. It’s kind of terrible,” Zhu said of the current state of simulation, referring to the gap between simulated and real-world environments. Daimon is developing tactile simulations that account for physical properties measured through real-world testing. The goal is to improve the fidelity of those simulations and make it easier to transfer learned capabilities to physical robots. The company has discussed collecting more than 10,000 hours of data, with its longer-term Daimon-Infinity initiative targeting more than 1 million hours of tactile embodied data. Zhu also emphasized the importance of working with companies developing robotic models and applications. “Doing everything ourselves was not enough,” he said. “Collaborating internationally in different downstream scenarios is really important.” That collaboration helps Daimon understand what other developers need from its sensors, data-collection devices, software, and evaluation tools. Credit: Daimon Robotics From tactile demonstrations to industrial applications Daimon is targeting manipulation tasks such as assembly and packaging, where robots must respond to physical contact rather than simply follow predetermined trajectories. A robot might need to determine whether a component is properly seated, detect when an object slips, or adjust its movements when a part behaves unexpectedly. Tactile feedback can help it respond to these conditions. The company demonstrated applications involving delicate manipulation at IROS 2026, including applying heat-transfer designs to tote bags and threading bracelets. It also showed a robot collecting and packaging broken glass, illustrating how models trained on data from varied scenarios can be prompted to perform specific tasks. Daimon uses its Umi device to collect data from human interactions. Zhu said the company’s demonstrations were powered by foundation models trained on data collected across multiple scenarios, rather than being built solely around individual robot demonstrations. The company has identified Lenovo Capital and Inovance Technology as key partners. Zhu said Daimon has also moved beyond proof-of-concept projects into industrial assembly lines and warehouses, although he declined to name specific customers because of nondisclosure agreements. The commercial test is whether tactile sensing and the models built around it can improve performance consistently in production environments, where robots must handle variations in objects, materials, and operating conditions. Moving beyond visual perception Daimon’s broader strategy centers on developing models that can use tactile information to understand and respond to physical interactions. Its Daimon-TWM effort focuses on a tactile-grounded world model intended to help robots reason about physical interactions, rather than relying on visual perception alone. Recognizing an object is only part of manipulation. A robot must also understand how its actions affect that object and adjust when the physical result differs from expectations. Tactile feedback can help close that loop by providing information about contact and the consequences of an action. Zhu described two roles for tactile sensing in robotic systems: helping models reason about physical properties and enabling rapid adjustments during contact-intensive tasks. The latter can require high-frequency feedback, with Daimon targeting control at 30 Hz. The company is also exploring how data collected through human interactions can help train models for different robot configurations, including humanoids and dual-arm manipulators. But collecting data and training models are only part of the problem. Developers must still demonstrate that these systems generalize across different objects, materials, robots, and operating conditions. Scaling touch for robotics The broader question facing the robotics industry is what infrastructure is needed to make physical AI work reliably outside controlled demonstrations. Companies are investing heavily in vision-language-action models, simulation, and large-scale robot training datasets. Touch adds another dimension, particularly for robots that must manipulate objects through physical contact. Daimon aims to build part of the infrastructure connecting sensing, data, simulation, and intelligence. Its strategy is to support the companies developing robotic systems rather than compete directly with them to build the next general-purpose robotic brain. Its success will depend on whether that approach measurably improves manipulation, reduces the effort required to develop new applications, and supports deployments across different industrial environments. Zhu was careful not to overstate the capabilities of today’s models. Even when trained on large datasets, he said, their ability to generalize remains limited. “The model is not as intelligent as we think,” Zhu said. “It has some generalization ability, but it was in-domain generalization sometimes.” He added that embodied-intelligence models are still in development, and that collecting data from similar tasks can help them generalize to new applications. For Daimon, the challenge is turning that emerging capability into reliable performance across a broader range of real-world tasks. global_items.title: Kodama raises $7M to bring robotics to forestry
global_items.summary: Kodama is working on automating forestry and logging equipment, starting with teleoperation and collecting valuable data on the way. The post Kodama raises $7M to bring robotics to forestry appeared first on The Robot Report .
global_items.articleText: Kodama initially focused on wildfire risk reduction in the western U.S., but it is now focusing on the timber industry in the southeastern U.S. | Source: Kodama Kodama Systems today said it has raised $7 million to bring physical AI to forestry. The company said it will use the latest funding to support commercial deployments, deepen OEM partnerships, and continue development of supervised autonomy capabilities for complex off-road environments. “Right now, we’re working with different forestry companies across the southeastern U.S,” Ben Pinfield, a go-to-market associate at Kodama, told The Robot Report . “We’re at a point where we’re scaling, integrating into new machine types, and developing more autonomy capabilities in forestry .” Kodama’s technology is already deployed in commercial logging operations across the southeastern U.S. Over the past six months, machines equipped with the company’s technology have moved more than 100,000 tons of timber across multiple states. “We’re focused on specifically plantation timber operations,” said Merritt Jenkins, co-founder and CEO of Kodama. “If we look more broadly, though, this is a tool for land management, and this is absolutely a tool that will be used in wildfire mitigation, from a forest thinning perspective, as well as wildfire suppression.” Including the latest funding, Kodama has raised a total of $14 million to date. Konvoy Ventures and Breakwater Ventures co-led the round. The round also included participation from Blue Forest Asset Management, NYA Ventures, Breakthrough Energy Ventures, Congruent Ventures, Dangerous Ventures, M1C, and others. The forestry industry faces tough conditions Forest contractors are facing a lot of challenges. Demand for timber, forest management, and wildfire-resilience work is rising, but each requires long hours at remote job sites. “If you’re a 20-something-year-old prospective logger thinking about entering the industry, you need to be on-site at 5:30 a.m., which means you’re usually leaving your home at like 4:00 or 4:30 in the morning,” Jenkins said. “Then, you’re in a machine for nine or 10 hours a day, driving over stumps and rocks and through ruts, beating up your body all day long. There are some loggers that we’ve spoken with who have gone through, for example, eight skidder operators in a year. It’s brutal turnover in this industry for this type of operator.” As fewer people go into the industry and more operators retire, it’s getting harder and harder to find experienced, reliable operators, and fewer people want to get into the industry. “For the heavy equipment operations, that [work] can be pretty rough on their bodies,” Pinfield said. “It’s like the bang just isn’t worth the buck as far as the physical trade-off for a lot of these operators. So, our customers are having a hard time hiring talent. Even when they are able to hire talent, a lot of times, it’s unreliable.” What does Kodama’s technology do on job sites? Kodama says its technology is currently running 10 to 14 hours a day on work sites. | Source: Kodama Kodama combines supervised autonomy with teleoperation , enabling machines to handle repeatable tasks while experienced operators remotely manage complex work and edge cases. The Sonora, Calif.-based company said this hybrid approach amplifies the capabilities of skilled operators and improves machine utilization. Kodama said it is currently working with skidders on logging sites. “When a group of trees are cut down, a skidder with a big claw called the grapple picks them up, and drags them to the landing where they are then loaded into trucks. It’s essentially moving these trees from one place to another,” Pinfield explained. “The ultimate goal is also working on the other machines that are in those fleets, which are the cutter and the loader.” Kodama said as it deploys more machines, its data advantage compounds through a continuous learning loop across equipment, operators, worksites, and forestry workflows. “Every day that we remotely operate the machine, we’re generating about a terabyte of training data,” Jenkins said. “Starting two and a half years ago, we took the explicit direction of starting with teleoperation, and incrementally adding autonomy, versus autonomy first with a teleoperations failover. That’s been absolutely the right decision. Now the amount of training data that we are generating across different operating environments throughout the southeast is massive.” Kodama works directly with existing OEMs Merritt Jenkins, co-founder and CEO of Kodama. | Source: Kodama Kodama is building its platform within the existing forestry-equipment ecosystem. This allows customers to adopt new operating capabilities while preserving the value of their existing machine fleets. Jenkins said the company is integrated with two of the three largest equipment manufacturers in the world. “It’s preferable to integrate with the OEMs because you can leverage all of their knowledge and all of the sensors and fault detection that are already on the machine,” Jenkins said. Autonomy retrofits are common in the construction world, but these are typically after-market kits. Jenkins said in the construction space, OEMs like Caterpillar create closed systems, so it isn’t possible to collaborate directly with the OEM. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! What has Kodama learned from job sites so far? Kodama has already had its technology deployed with customers in the southeast U.S. for the past two years. Pinfield said the company has been working with a customer in Georgia for over a year. “It’s always a learning process. Every logging site is a little bit different, with different terrain and a different crew that you have to work with and introduce this new technology to them,” Pinfield said. Among the biggest benefits of automation for these site operators are reliable and consistent operations. The team has also seen safety improvements with the technology. “Every person I spoke to on the logging sites has some kind of crazy story about how they know someone in the cab who flipped the machine, or got hurt, or a tree went flying. So, taking them out of the cab and having it be remote controlled or autonomous is a lot safer,” Pinfield said. Looking ahead, the company plans to expand deployments and use the data it gathers to improve productivity on job sites. “Right now, it’s several people coordinating via CB radio,” Jenkins said. “We know the real time location of our machines. We have metrics of productivity, fuel use, and the shock and vibration on the machines. So, we believe that we can eventually further optimize these sites in terms of how the machines are used and how they coordinate with each other.” About The Author Brianna Wessling Brianna Wessling is an Associate Editor, Robotics, WTWH Media. She joined WTWH Media in November 2021, after graduating from the University of Kansas with degrees in Journalism and English. She covers a wide range of robotics topics, but specializes in women in robotics, robotics in healthcare, and space robotics. She can be reached at [email protected] Tell Us What You Think! global_items.title: NVIDIA Advances Agentic Security for Media, From European Public Service Broadcasting to Global Content Production
global_items.summary: At a creative industry event that took place today in Berlin — hosted in collaboration with Adobe, Bertelsmann, NVIDIA and UFA — the latest advancements in intelligent media were on display. Key to the news: the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) is collaborating with NVIDIA to expand its sovereign framework with cloud, open models and integration […]
global_items.articleText: At a creative industry event that took place today in Berlin — hosted in collaboration with Adobe , Bertelsmann , NVIDIA and UFA — the latest advancements in intelligent media were on display. Key to the news: the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) is collaborating with NVIDIA to expand its sovereign framework with cloud, open models and integration partners, while Adobe Frame.io is accelerating video agent search capabilities with NVIDIA GPUs, helping German TV and film producer UFA find the right moments faster. Read more about both announcements below. Sovereign Clouds and Open Models Built for European Broadcasters The EBU and NVIDIA are expanding the sovereign standards they introduced last year for European public service media. The initiative now brings in sovereign cloud providers, open model developers and systems integrators to define how broadcasters can deploy agents while keeping control of their data, infrastructure, models and security. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements The EBU is the world’s leading alliance of public service media, with over 115 member organizations in more than 55 countries reaching over 1 billion people. As agents move into newsrooms, production and audience services, those broadcasters need a foundation that protects editorial independence, data sovereignty and national resilience. The expanded initiative is turning those principles into deployable services. It’ll define requirements and reference architectures for where workloads run, how data is governed, which models power services and how systems stay secure throughout their lifecycle. “These standards give EBU members a shared foundation to strengthen resilience, retain control and deliver accountable advanced services that sustain audience trust,” said Antonio Arcidiacono, chief technology and innovation officer at the EBU . Cloud providers will map the standards to sovereign deployment options: Microsoft will bring expertise from Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, including Azure Local and Foundry Local, so broadcasters can process sensitive editorial material locally and keep critical services running when external connectivity is down. Nebius offers a platform for broadcasters to train, fine-tune and run their own models on European infrastructure. Open models give broadcasters the visibility to inspect, evaluate and adapt AI for local languages, archives and editorial policies. NVIDIA Nemotron open models provide a foundation broadcasters can customize for domain-specific applications and public-service requirements. “Sovereign cloud infrastructure and open models can help Europe’s public service media innovate while protecting data, editorial independence and cultural diversity,” said Delphine Ernotte, CEO of France Télévisions and president of the EBU . Media-specific consulting and systems integration provided from Qvest and other system integrators to ensure that reference architectures are practical, interoperable and deployable in real world broadcast environments. Adobe Frame.io Speeds Video Search With NVIDIA Accelerated Computing Also at the event, Adobe is highlighting its latest enhancements that help creatives search through video data faster. Adobe is using NVIDIA accelerated computing to help creative teams find and work with video content faster. Its GPU-accelerated search pipeline uses NVIDIA NVDEC for video decoding, TensorRT for optimized AI inference and the CUDA platform for preprocessing and embedding generation. Adobe is also advancing GPU-accelerated media ingest using NVIDIA NVENC and NVDEC to accelerate video encoding and decoding, helping production teams process growing media libraries more efficiently. The results: about 5x faster embedding generation, up to 4x higher throughput and up to 5x lower latency for search processing. A new two-frame-per-second proxy, about 80% smaller than the 360p version it replaces, cuts storage and transfer while keeping the visual detail search needs. That speed matters for UFA , one of Germany’s leading film and TV producers. It delivers more than 3,500 hours of programming a year, including the daily drama “Gute Zeiten, schlechte Zeiten.” When editors build a recap or flashback, they may need a specific reaction or unresolved exchange from as far back as 15 years — something file names and folders can’t surface. Frame.io semantic search finds moments inside videos by concept, action or setting, and hybrid search adds notes, transcripts and approval status. An editor can search for “a character looking concerned,” narrow by character name and filter to approved footage, then move straight into review. The work is part of a broader Adobe and NVIDIA collaboration that also spans Adobe Substance 3D, Firefly Foundry and 3D digital twin workflows for enterprises. Learn more about NVIDIA technologies for media and entertainment . global_items.articleText: Gazebo PMC Meeting Minutes 2026-10-19 - Gazebo PMC - Open Robotics Discourse Gazebo PMC Meeting Minutes 2026-10-19 Gazebo Gazebo PMC gazebo , meeting , pmc azeey October 20, 2026, 9:03pm 1 Hi Gazebo Community! This week’s meeting was held on 2026-10-19T18:00:00Z and the following is a summary: PMC Business Approved adding Luca Della Vedova as a mentee PMC member. New agenda items Community Meeting : A reminder for this week’s community meeting on Scalable Multi-Robot Simulation in ROS 2 and Gazebo , featuring multi-robot simulation, namespaces, and automatic bridging. Please note the change in date and time this month (7:00 PM Pacific) to better accommodate the Asia-Pacific region. Fuel Server Outage & Maintenance : The Fuel server experienced downtime over the weekend due to high memory consumption triggered by crawler traffic downloading models in parallel. The server was restarted, and backend changes are being prepared to avoid loading full models into RAM along with an updated deployment mechanism (fuel-server#25 ). Auto-Merge & Required CI Checks : Maintainers are reminded to verify which CI checks are required before enabling GitHub auto-merge. A recent Fortress backport (gz-sim#4076 ) auto-merged despite failing builds because only the DCO check was required, and had to be reverted (gz-sim#4079 ). Branch protection rules are being updated in terraform_github_repos#10 to require Jenkins and GitHub Actions CI checks. Lightweight 2D Physics Engine Exploration (Box2D vs. TPE) : Discussed experimenting with Box2D as a physics engine plugin to support very large-scale planar simulations with hundreds of robots requiring only collisions and basic kinematic motion. Compared against the existing Trivial Physics Engine (TPE), which currently lacks joint support; a deeper comparison between Box2D and extending TPE will be conducted. Updates Simulation, Physics & C++20 Migration Bullet-Featherstone Kinematic Mode : Merged the full set of PRs enabling kinematic mode in Bullet-Featherstone on Rotary, with backports planned after verification on a demo world: Enforce position limits on kinematically driven joints (gz-physics#1118 ) Fix toggling links between kinematic and dynamic (gz-physics#1122 ) Kinematic base velocity for links with a CoM offset (gz-physics#1123 ) Fix force-torque sensor in hybrid kinematic/dynamic modes (gz-physics#1124 ) Fix root joint position and velocity (gz-physics#1125 ) ECM Batch Queries : Merged runtime-typed EntityComponentManager (ECM) batch queries and exposed them to Python (gz-sim#4006 ). C++20 Migration : Continuing work on gz-cmake#580 to avoid hardcoding the C++ standard so builds follow the exported target standard. PRs are in review for sdformat examples (sdformat#1733 ), gz-sim plugin examples and tutorials (gz-sim#4086 ), and the DART ContactSurface check in gz-physics (gz-physics#1134 ). Rendering, Sensors & Transport Ogre 1.12 Migration : The large Ogre 1.12 migration PR was split into stacked PRs for easier review (gz-rendering PRs ). While general custom shaders were fixed, custom terrain heightmap shaders remain broken due to upstream class removals in Ogre 1.12; the PMC agreed to merge without custom terrain shader support if a quick fix is not found, and request examples from users if needed later. PixelBuffer API Adaptations : Backports adapting gz-sensors to the PixelBuffer API (gz-sensors#674 ) have been merged for Harmonic and Fortress, and are in review for Jetty (gz-sensors#677 ) and Ionic (gz-sensors#678 ) ahead of upcoming point releases. Zenoh CI in gz-sim : A PR is in review to run Ubuntu Resolute CI tests a second time using Zenoh on gz-sim main (gz-sim#4085 ). The team agreed that gz-transport should fail explicitly when Zenoh is selected via environment variable but not compiled in, rather than silently falling back to ZeroMQ. Web & Documentation Gazebo Web Ecosystem : Ongoing work to modernize the gazebosim-app web frontend (gazebosim-app PRs ). We are also evaluating the feasibility of rewriting gzweb in Rust using the Bevy engine to improve performance, realism, and modern SDFormat support. Maintainer Guidelines : Merged documentation updates covering backport timing, downstream testing tradeoffs, and prerelease version bump review policies (docs#723 ). Infrastructure, Packaging & Release Tooling macOS 26 (Tahoe) & Homebrew : Tahoe bottling is in progress (homebrew-simulation#3599 ). The primary hurdle is compiling ogre1.9 without the Apple Graphics Library (AGL, removed in macOS 26), for which a community contributed patch is in review (homebrew-simulation#3615 ). Investigated flaky Homebrew build failures on Harmonic and Fortress caused by a Doxygen bug (homebrew-simulation#3616 ); mitigation is complete for Harmonic and in review for Fortress. Pixi on macOS : Prerequisites for supporting Pixi on macOS are in review (release-tools#1566 , release-tools#1568 ). Discussed the possibility of eventually phasing out Homebrew bottle builds if Pixi provides a smooth macOS developer experience, while keeping the Homebrew tap available. Release & CI Tooling : An automated changelog generation tool is up for review (release-tools#1447 ). A PR to skip Linux CI-pr Jenkins jobs when modified files match an ignore list is awaiting final updates (release-tools#1558 ). Build warning fixes are in review for gz-physics (gz-physics#1127 ) and gz-cmake (gz-cmake#603 ). rosdistro-extension work is underway to generate binary packages for testing distributions and handle automatic sourcing of setup.bash from child to parent workspaces. As always, the meeting notes are available at Gazebo PMC meeting weekly agenda - Google Docs . Battle Drones—a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer 20th October 2026 My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones (play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I’m somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to “Make it a LOT more fun”. It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here’s what I’ve built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer . I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. Here’s a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser: Features so far include: 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units—all 3D models, which you can browse here Fog of war Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles Six maps , across five biomes—temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical A random map generator Skirmish mode —red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map Last Stand mode —one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer Crate drops with bonus resources In-game music that responds to events—it gets more intense as fighting breaks out Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad) AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other The Goliath —a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base Mutators that add extra rules or twists A “Daily Op” challenge Ranks and achievements (Medals ) Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong How I built this Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded—I’ve reviewed almost none of the code, and it’s built in a language (TypeScript) that I’ve hardly used myself. I’ve playtested it quite a bit though, and it’s been through a large number of iterations since I started the project. Here’s a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts. v1: the initial prototype I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July: We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions Here’s a shared transcript . I’d given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites. You can try v1 here —it looked like this: It’s recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against. This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn’t any fun to play. Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn’t even realize this until several iterations later! v2: full sprites The second version (try v2 here ) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the “AI vs. AI” mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself. Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI’s image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder. v3: varied terrain It still wasn’t much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it: Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain. This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here . Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here —it looks like this: This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn’t very fun to play though—I found myself getting bored pretty quickly. v4: the fun update So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can’t actually make something that’s genuinely compelling to play. I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone: This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun. This time I was running in Ultracode mode , where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs “dynamic workflows”, described in their docs as: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once. This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn’t get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular. You can try v4 here —it looks like this: I had Claude write its own release notes —here are the highlights: Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that’s losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play. Openers : pick Blitz, Industry or Air Wing before the clock starts. Call-down powers : Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod and the Sky Hammer orbital strike. Objectives and salvage : Uplink relays, supply drops and wrecks worth scrap. Feel : combat juice, adaptive music, unit voices and an announcer. Command : battle alerts, game speed, saved squads and touch placement. New modes : Last Stand survival waves and an 8-mission Ops campaign. Progression : heroes, an after-action report with awards, a career, 7 mutators and a Daily Op. Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%. Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features. v5: Battle Drones goes 3D After the success of Ultracode at “Make it a LOT more fun”, I decided to be more ambitious: Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version : The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code. v6 (play v6 here ) added some more visual polish. v7 (play v7 ) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a “Condor” troop carrying aircraft. v8: Archipelago I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game—it really had been a case of me saying “make it more fun” and “add visual polish” for the past few releases. I’d noticed that the AI didn’t use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often—there wasn’t a great strategic reason to use them. It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map. This resulted in my longest prompt yet: Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles. To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor. Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board. The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different places I want to encourage a battle over uplinks. The map should be the times the size of other maps - still square First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications You get to design a new biome for this The result was the tropical Archipelago map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It’s definitely the most fun map to play, once you’ve got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting—it now looks like this: v10: Goliath, and agent battles I decided to add giant robot mechs to the game—think Jaegers from Pacific Rim , or Titans from Warhammer 40,000. Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude: Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnoughts or titans from W20K - how could we do this in a way that enhanced gameplay, kept things balanced, added unique twist? Don't overthink this yet Let's keep brainstorming. I like the idea that it's a mobile base - that can accept harvested scrap and can have buildings built near it (even if it later moves on) and can produce infantry units too. An interaction with condor would be neat but I don't know what that could be. Idea: as it gets damage it loses the ability to fire some weapons - by default it has eye laser (like lancers) and arm canons (like titan) and two shoulder mounted mortars, plus machine guns similar to a squad of troops Damage knocks out mortars and then laser - it always has guns. You can't build next to a building that was only put there because of the mech, you need the mech there for off-base building and only within three squares of it [...] Lets do two condors can carry the mech The end result is really cool . Your browser does not support HTML video. Goliaths can be constructed using a Gantry—a building that can only be created after first building a Fab, Bay, Airpad, and Tech Lab. You can see the Goliath under construction, and it then walks out from the Gantry and can march around the map. Goliaths can “anchor”, which digs them into the ground. In their anchored state they can act as a new HQ, constructing infantry units and additional buildings in a new area. Two Condor aircraft can hook onto a Goliath, at which point it can be flown around the map! The game now ends when you destroy the enemy’s HQ building and any Goliaths they might have built. There are also a couple of mutators relating to Goliaths: Goliath Armada starts each side with four airborne Goliaths (each with a pair of Condors) and no other units. global_items.title: My obituary for programming
global_items.summary: My obituary for programming Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code: Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real. Via lobste.rs Tags: programming , careers , ai , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , deep-blue

global_items.title: DeepInfer: High-performance inference framework for DeepSeek models
global_items.articleText: main Branches Tags Go to file Code Open more actions menu Latest commit History 3 Commits 3 Commits Folders and files Name Name Last commit message Last commit date csrc csrc deep_cluster deep_cluster deepinfer deepinfer doc doc eval eval examples examples scripts scripts tests tests vendor vendor .clang-format .clang-format .gitignore .gitignore .gitmodules .gitmodules CONTRIBUTING.md CONTRIBUTING.md LICENSE LICENSE Makefile Makefile README.md README.md build.sh build.sh pyproject.toml pyproject.toml requirements-ascend.txt requirements-ascend.txt requirements-dev.txt requirements-dev.txt requirements-nvidia.txt requirements-nvidia.txt requirements.txt requirements.txt setup.py setup.py View all files Repository files navigation DeepInfer DeepInfer is the high-performance inference framework that powers DeepSeek's large-scale production services. This open-source release provides offline inference with the core features needed for serving at scale. Supported models: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Supported features: Optimized kernels, model and sampler runtime Parallelism: Attention DP / balanced CP, MoE EP + EPLB DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification SWA bounded replay Asynchronous scheduling (zero-overhead batch scheduler) Batch-invariant inference Deterministic sampling Structured outputs Feature details and configuration Optimized kernels: FlashMLA , DeepGEMM , DeepEP , TileKernels , DeepSelect , and custom TileLang kernels . DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification: accelerate decoding with draft tokens and use confidence estimates to schedule verification. Set DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=1 ; DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE controls the maximum draft length (default: 5). Decoder SWA bounded replay: reduce decoder prefill work by replaying only a bounded suffix. Set DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact and DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140 for the default V4.1 settings; the retained suffix must cover the SWA window plus the maximum backtracking length. Asynchronous scheduling: overlap CPU batch scheduling with device execution. Enabled by default. Batch-invariant inference: keep model results identical across different batch compositions. Enable with DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 (NVIDIA only). Deterministic sampling: produce identical outputs for identical input tokens and sampling parameters. Set DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0 and pass a fixed seq_seed to SamplingParams (NVIDIA only). Structured outputs: constrain generation to a regex, JSON schema, or EBNF grammar. Pass so_args={"schema_type": ..., "schema": ...} to SamplingParams ; see examples . Supported hardware: NVIDIA SM100 GPUs Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs Required for a complete inference service (not included in this release): A KV cache system VE/Prefill/Decode disaggregation (most required engine functionality is already implemented) Load balancing across data-parallel replicas for both prefill and decode Getting started Prerequisites Linux GCC >= 13.0 Python 3.12 CUDA 13 (NVIDIA only) CANN 9.2 (Ascend only) Build from source Before building DeepInfer, please create and activate an empty Python 3.12 environment. # Use `ascend` instead for the Ascend platform # Keep it exported in the environment where you run DeepInfer export DEEPINFER_ACCELERATOR=nvidia ./build.sh Offline inference The default checkpoint, deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 , is downloaded into the Hugging Face cache on the first run; set DEEPINFER_HF_MODEL_DIR=/path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 to run from a local copy instead. python examples/offline_inference.py See examples for details. Performance benchmarks Prefill Decode Measured on 4 SM100 GPUs for prefill and 64 for decode — each within one scale-up domain. To reproduce the benchmarks, see run_sweep.sh . Evaluation benchmarks See eval/README.md . License DeepInfer is released under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE for details. Acknowledgments DeepInfer was originally built primarily on vLLM , with additional inspiration from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM . We thank their developers. global_items.title: Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins
global_items.articleText: Related articles Claude discovers a novel enzyme system with CRISPR-like repeats View more Summary: As part of our work experimenting with how Claude can help accelerate drug discovery, we asked an internal research model to design minibinders (small proteins that attach tightly to a target) against scorpion neurotoxins. Claude worked from our prompt and four follow-ups, which we developed in collaboration with the financial investment research firm Citrini Research. Teams at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience experimentally tested 211 designs for binding. Of these, 17 met our criteria. We’re releasing all 211 designs and their data as a resource for the field. In August, we showed how Claude designed protein minibinders after being given a single prompt. A month before we released those results, a team from Citrini Research had approached us with an interesting question: could Claude (and AI drug discovery more generally) enable a group of motivated nonexperts to tackle a genuine problem in human health? Members of our life science research team set out to answer this, first by brainstorming problems with Claude. We landed on asking for Claude’s help designing novel protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins, with the hope that they could one day be used to develop a scorpion antivenom. Scorpions sting 1.2 million people or more every year, resulting in more than 3,250 deaths, mostly among children in parts of the world with limited access to medical care. New treatments are expensive to make, and are also unlikely to earn back the cost of developing them. With so little investment, scorpion envenomation has been described as a neglected tropical disease. We started by giving Claude the same prompt we’d used in our earlier protein-binder study, after modifying it with Citrini.1 Over the next 64 hours, an internal research model, operating within Claude Science, worked mainly autonomously, although we directed its work with four follow-ups. Under our supervision, Claude analyzed the research data, generated the figures, and drafted the final report. Claude’s design campaign produced 17 protein binders that each bind to one of four scorpion neurotoxins that are known to be dangerous to humans. Throughout the process, Claude generated 318,484 protein designs and selected 180 of them for testing. Our team added 31 more, with Claude’s help. Our partners at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, two contract research organizations (CROs), lab-tested all 211 designs to see if they would bind to the toxins they were designed against, and 17 designs met our criteria for a binder. We have not confirmed whether these binders neutralize scorpion venom in a cellular environment, so we do not claim to have produced an antivenom. We sent Claude’s work to two outside experts, Susana Vázquez Torres and Timothy P. Jenkins, who said they felt this work was a promising first step. If AI can now design credible binders against several hard-to-target toxins in days and they can be confirmed in the lab within weeks, this could, in theory, speed up discovery for envenomation and other neglected diseases. The challenge, as always, is turning those binders into safe, affordable, and widely accessible drugs. We share more detail in our technical report , and are making all 211 designs and their data available . Designing a binder against almost any target no longer seems unrealistic. We can now obtain very tight binders remarkably quickly, and binding itself is no longer the main bottleneck. For venomous animals such as snakes and scorpions, whose bites and stings kill or seriously injure large numbers of people, particularly in underserved regions, the real impact will come from tackling the parts of the therapeutic pipeline that go beyond binding. The challenge is to use these extraordinary tools to develop molecules that can become real drugs, ones that are safe, affordable, and widely accessible. Susana Vázquez Torres , Postdoctoral Researcher, Structural Biology Programme, Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO), Madrid, Spain. Designing de novo binders against five toxins from four species of scorpions Scorpion venom contains multiple protein neurotoxins. The neurotoxins that are most likely to harm or kill humans attach to sodium channels , large proteins embedded in the membranes of nerve cells that allow them to fire. When sodium channels are disrupted, nerves fire at the wrong time—this releases large amounts of stress chemicals, like adrenaline. In severe cases, this can cause heart failure and excess fluid buildup in the lungs, occasionally resulting in death. There are some antivenoms available for scorpion stings. They’re generally made using the antibodies of immunized animals, a process that can take months. Venom is milked from thousands of scorpions and used to immunize horses; scientists then purify the resulting antibodies from the horses’ blood. Traditional antivenoms can work when given early, but they’re usually effective for only a small number of neurotoxins. They’re also expensive to produce, and in many regions are costly or in short supply. De novo design offers a potential solution. A binder is a molecule that attaches tightly to a specific target; antibodies are one natural example. In principle, a binder that targets the part of a neurotoxin that latches onto sodium channels could stop the toxin from reaching the channel. In de novo design, protein binders are generated from scratch against a specific target. These binders are designed computationally and can be optimized for druglike properties such as potency and stability, which could make them easier to supply in regions where stings most often occur. Our approach was inspired by an earlier effort that designed de novo proteins that neutralized snake neurotoxins and protected mice. To our knowledge, no de novo -designed binders against scorpion neurotoxins have been described. For this campaign, we chose to target five scorpion-venom neurotoxins across four regions: Mexico (Cn2), Brazil (Ts1), North Africa (AaH I and AaH II), and the Middle East (LqhIII). We also chose to aim the designs at each toxin’s channel-binding site. Claude picked the toxin structures to use for design by searching the Protein Data Bank (PDB) as well as the AlphaFold database (AFDB). For each toxin, it selected five hotspots , specific amino acid positions on the toxin that its binder designs were meant to latch onto. We were primarily wondering if Claude could design binders against individual toxins. But we were also curious if Claude could design binders that targeted multiple toxins. There’s a practical reason for trying to design multitoxin binders, namely that it would reduce the number of molecules needed for a universal antivenom cocktail—which would be the most cost-effective and regionally neutral treatment. We selected these five scorpion toxins (Cn2, Ts1, AaH I, AaH II, and LqhIII) as a challenging test of multitoxin design: they share one fold for the overall shape of the protein, but any two are only 26% to 62% identical in their amino acid sequences. To see how far Claude could go, we asked it to design four kinds of binders: binders against each of the five toxins individually; binders that targeted the β-family toxins Ts1 and Cn2; binders that targeted the α-family toxins AaH II, AaH I, and LqhIII; and binders that targeted all five toxins simultaneously. Designing credible binders against five toxins in parallel, in a matter of days, is a great showcase of the AI-driven paradigm shift we are seeing in therapeutic discovery. This is especially true for neglected diseases such as animal envenomings, which have been largely starved of innovation due to low commercial incentives. Being able to agentically tackle the uniquely broad target space across animal toxins provides a significant speed-up in discovery, and brings realistic therapeutic solutions much closer. Timothy P. Jenkins , Associate Professor, Technical University of Denmark. Claude ran the design campaign with considerable autonomy Our initial prompt defined the neurotoxin targets, the protein design and folding tools, and the rules for novelty, scoring, and filtering. Beyond choosing the structures and amino acid hotspots, Claude also set the quality thresholds a design had to clear, decided how much to lean on each available design tool, and developed the strategies for designing binders against multiple toxins. Ultimately, Claude used 12 design tools to generate 318,484 designs, filtering out any that resembled a toxin or a known protein. Claude co-folded and screened 553,052 design-toxin pairs, predicting each pair’s structure as one complex. Sixty-four hours after we gave Claude our initial prompt, it produced its final list of 180 designs. The campaign used on the order of 10,000 GPU hours.2 Claude worked autonomously for 24 hours following our first prompt. Its results encouraged us to prompt Claude to continue its campaign and look for better designs. Our follow-up prompts were mainly focused on directing Claude to design a multitoxin binder. Claude selected most of the 180 designs—including our strongest binder (Cn2-B1)—only after our third follow-up. At our request, Claude sent the protein sequences to Twist Bioscience (in emails indicating they were written by Claude), which produced the proteins in order to see how well they would bind to the toxins. We later worked with Claude to add another 31 designs, increasing the total to 211 designs: 60 designs against a single toxin (12 per toxin), 30 designs against the two β-family toxins, 30 designs against the three α-family toxins, and 91 designs against all five toxins. Of the 211 designs our teams assessed, 17 met our criteria for a binder, each against a single toxin. None of the designs made against multiple toxins met our criteria for more than one. (Beyond being limited by its current capabilities, there could be many explanations for why Claude struggled with this, including our prompting, the limitations of available design tools, and even the biological feasibility of multitoxin design.) Seven designs were binders against Cn2, four against AaH II, four against AaH I, and two against LqhIII. Among the 60 single-toxin designs, 11 were binders (18%). This rate is consistent with typical protein design campaigns, including our previous work. Testing Claude's designs in the lab After completing the campaign, we sent the designs to Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience to test them for binding. Each group produced the designs in their labs, but in different formats. Adaptyv Bio expressed them in a cell-free system , which uses protein-making machinery extracted from bacteria rather than living cells. Twist Bioscience expressed the designs in mammalian cells (in this case, human kidney cells) as fusions to Fc , the stem of an antibody. These are complementary ways to measure the underlying binding process, and we combined them in order to improve confidence in our results. Both labs measured binding by surface plasmon resonance (SPR), in which a toxin flows over the design while the SPR instrument tracks in real time how quickly a toxin binds to and detaches from it. The resulting trace, called a sensorgram, produces a measurement known as the dissociation constant (KD), which is a measurement for binding strength (or affinity ). The lower the KD, the tighter the binding. When it came to evaluating the resulting designs, we set out strict criteria for labeling a design a binder against a toxin. The design needed to be a hit at both labs3 —that is, it needed to show evidence of binding against that toxin in every replicate, and every KD needed to be 1 µM or tighter. We also required that the design show no signal against CLEC12A, an unrelated human protein used to measure off-target binding or “stickiness.” Claude’s Cn2 binders likely bind the same site as a toxin-neutralizing antibody Antibodies and nan

global_items.title: Publish fake stats, get cited in LLMs
global_items.articleText: Publish stats, get cited: The tactic that put my data all over the web - Peec AI Publish stats, get cited: The tactic that put my data all over the web Metehan Yesilyurt GEO Researcher Oct 7, 2026 GEO Know-How Inside the page Want more of Peec AI? Subscribe to our weekly newsletter. Subscribe Share this What I learned about AI search when I made up 50,000 stats that got cited by ChatGPT... About 7 months ago, I launched a website with 50,000 statistics. Every one of them was fake. Google has forgotten the site exists and deindexed the pages, but ChatGPT hasn't. Since the website went live 7 months ago, it has sent more than 10,000 AI sessions its way. And now more than 330 referring domains, including Shopify, Bluehost, and DHL, link to the site. Its made-up numbers have also ended up in an academic paper and in a bank's investment research. At Peec AI and in the industry, we talk about GEO and SEO every day, and we keep looking for new tactics. I’ve been working on this stats page one for a long time, sharing pieces of it publicly along the way. Of course, it’s experimental, but the results have been hard to ignore. Where the idea for publishing fake statistics came from The impetus to seed a site with statistics came out of long-running research I've been doing on LLMs, relevance engineering, and grounding (credit to the iPullRank team, Dan Petrovic, and Wil Reynolds). In the course of my work, I noticed a pattern: as more teams write time-sensitive and breaking content with LLMs, those LLMs have to look for (seemingly) reliable data during their research to fill the gaps in their knowledge. Statistics are often exactly what they’re looking for. Most GEO advice focuses on one moment: getting your brand into the AI answer. This experiment looks at what happens after the answer, when people take that output and use it, putting it into presentations, adding it to a shopping list, and yes, publishing it on their website. I didn't come up with the idea for this experiment alone. Hat tip to Seer Interactive, who already published an eye-opening study in August 2025 that got a few thoughts bouncing around in my head. Several months later, those thoughts came together and finally made it to the top of my to-do list. In March 2026, I started working on building the site that would let me test my ideas. The setup: a website and 50,000 made-up stats, created in one day Quick context for anyone who wasn’t following along in real time as I ran this experiment: I bought a brand-new domain, stateglobe.com, and generated 50,000 statistics pages in a single day with GPT-4.1. The site purports to provide stats on SEO, content marketing, social media, e-commerce, and web technology from 200 countries. Except every number was totally invented. I never checked a single one. I pushed them to the site with a basic AI web design template. This cost me around $30. Later, I added 15,000 listicles on top of the statistics. That was about $20 more, so all in all, this is an experiment that came in at the very low price of about $50. The reaction when I first shared it was wild. When my friend Kevin featured it in Growth Memo , it reached a much bigger audience. I think people responded so enthusiastically to this work because it showed great results while also speaking to the fears people have about what ends up in AI search results. What happened Google buried the site almost immediately When I launched the site, traffic, indexing, and engagement were initially going really well. Using indexer tools, I got almost the entire site indexed within a week, and it started to appear in Google results. Then two Google updates came out right after launch, and my Google visibility collapsed. I've been invisible on Google for many months now. Indexed pages bounce between 5 and 20 impressions. At one point, I got curious and created a subdomain to see if I could increase impressions, but it didn't really help. Other than that, I haven't touched the site. Some pages might even fail to load now and then. I don't know. But when I sat down to write this, I checked the crawl data in Cloudflare after 7 months. In the last 30 days alone, the site got more than 600,000 requests from bots. Around 72,000 of them came from ChatGPT-User. That is the agent ChatGPT uses to open a page in real time while answering someone. So these are not training crawls. Each one is ChatGPT fetching a fake statistics page to answer a real question. Unlike Google, ChatGPT never stopped pulling from the site And when I say, “never stopped,” I mean ChatGPT really never stopped. After 7 months, the site now has 330+ referring domains According to Ahrefs and Semrush, the site has links from 330+ other sites. That includes well-known brands like Shopify, DHL, and Bluehost. With strong Google performance, the numbers might have been even better. ChatGPT is still citing it to this day Google may have forgotten about the site, but ChatGPT clearly hasn’t. The site is still earning citations and traffic more than 7 months after launch. If you've read Tomek's ChatGPT Index research , you're lucky, because it’s a great intro to how ChatGPT search works. If you haven't, add it to your reading list right now, because it helps explain why my website has been living in ChatGPT/OpenAI Index for so long. A completely made-up website still performing so well is shocking. Since March, GA4 shows 10,000+ sessions from ChatGPT alone, and Cloudflare shows the site has high marks for retrieval. I didn’t include direct sessions in overall visits, because it mostly looks like bot traffic. Remember the dead internet theory! Right after I joined Peec in June 2026, I also set up a visibility dashboard in our tool to track a few prompts. Performance for them is still strong. On October 7, stateglobe.com was ranked second for visibility on these prompts, behind only data powerhouse Statista. Retrieval is not ranking The constant retrieval is the first big lesson: ranking on Google and being retrievable by an LLM are two different problems. When ChatGPT searches, it doesn't just copy Google's top 10. It rewrites your prompt into its own sub-queries (called fanout queries), pulls candidates from its search sources and its own cache, reranks them, and then opens a handful of pages to ground the answer. A page can be invisible on Google and still perform well in every one of those LLM steps. StateGlobe is a good example. While Google dropped it, the AI retrieval bots kept coming back. For GEO, this means Google rankings are only one signal, not the whole picture. If you only track Google, you are missing a channel that can work even when Google says “no.” Fake data turned into real citations You’d expect that if a site performs well with information retrieval tools, its information would begin to appear out in the wild. And you would be right. StateGlobe was built entirely on fake data, using the cheapest model available and a prompt that was nothing more than a list of countries and topics plus two sentences. Nevertheless, the output was… …cited in an academic paper… …used in investment research by Qatar's largest financial group… …cited by an economics publication in India… …and used as a source in a research report from a Canadian influencer community. Note that these are only the citations that linked back to the StateGlobe site. Presumably, many more used the data without a link. The uncomfortable implication: citation laundering On day one, a fake number on StateGlobe had zero authority. It was a random stat on a brand-new domain. Then an academic paper cited it. Then a bank. Now the next person, or the next model, that finds this number sees a stat with a source. And that source is cited by serious institutions. The fake data certainly didn't become true, but every citation made it look more trustworthy. It has the potential to get worse: after so much retrieval and citation, these pages end up in web crawls, and web crawls end up in training data (I hope it hasn’t!). A number that started as a GPT-4.1 guess can become something the next model "knows." This points to the larger risk suggested by this experiment, and it's why I'm sharing this as research, not as a playbook for fake content. Verifying sources should become an essential part of writers’ and researchers’ workflows. Lastly, we tried running our experiment with real data Once I began working at Peec, I decided to try a version of this test again. As the GEO Research team, we talked through the results up until that point and quickly launched a simple new page. This time, there were no made-up numbers, and we checked every stat and properly cited its source. You can view it here: peec.ai/ai-search-geo-statistics . Almost immediately, sites we suspect use AI to write their content started linking to us. For the second time, using a second site, earning links by publishing statistical content proved that a hypothetically strong tactic worked in reality. Lessons learned Why publishing statistics leads to LLM citations The two tests show that LLMs have a strong preference for seeking out statistics when asked to write articles. The mechanism is simple: More and more content is written with LLMs. When an LLM writes, it researches the appropriate topic. When the LLM hits a gap, it looks for a number to fill it. The reasons behind this process are equally clear. Research means fanout queries asking for statistics When a prompt requires research, the model breaks it into sub-queries, adds modifiers like "statistics," "data," "report," or the current year (if also requested in the prompt text). If someone asks for the model to compose a blog post about remote work, the model will search for "remote work statistics 2026." Pages that optimize for what models search rather than for what humans type will appear more often in LLM results. A number looks like evidence that can fill knowledge gaps When a model is asked to draft a piece of writing, a citation to a page that says "Remote work is growing" adds little authority and remains vague. If that page instead says "X% of employees work remotely at least once a week," there’s suddenly something that is specific, quotable, and additive. When a model grounds an answer, a specific number is the most useful thing it can find. These numbers look like evidence, though as this experiment proves, sometimes they aren’t. The model doesn’t check the number A search-grounded piece of LLM-written content has a tight budget for latency and cost. The system fetches a few pages, pulls the relevant passages, and starts to write. Fact-checking doesn’t happen anywhere in the process. Verifying a single statistic would mean finding independent sources, comparing them, and resolving conflicts. Across billions of prompts by millions of users, the costs in both time and money would add up, making verification too slow and too expensive for practical purposes. To get around this, LLMs use rerankers that score relevance, but not truth. That means if a passage matches the query and looks authoritative, it gets used. Statistics have a built-in freshness that models like I've written before about ChatGPT's recency bias in how it scores sources. Statistics pages contain the year in the title, the headings, and the URL. Three built-in signals to the model that what’s on the page is fresh. How to build a statistics page the right way The two tests I ran show that statistics pages are a very powerful way to get your content cited by LLMs. While I absolutely do not recommend coming up with bogus data, you can use the learnings from our small test to create your own pages with real data. Here's what worked for us at Peec and what I would do if I were making a statistics page again. Make one claim per sentence. Each stat should make sense on its own, out of context. Retrieval doesn’t work on pages, but rather on passages. If a number needs the paragraph above it to make sense, it probably won't get pul
